Operating Systems 2
☆ Reproducer Synthesis for AI-Reported Bugs in the Linux Kernel
Xiao Wu, Yunbo Ni, Hao Sun, Yuanyuan Yuan, Shaohua Li
Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC. We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a new review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution shows what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.

♻ ☆ safeL4: Rethinking Safe-Language-Based Single Address Space Microkernels ASPLOS 2027
Zheyuan Xu, Xiaobei Zhang, Zihan Li, Zekai Nie, Guangtao Zhu, Zhuang Lu, Qianying Zhang, Shijun Zhao, Haibo Chen, Rui Hou
Microkernels provide good features such as high security, safety, and flexibility, but their reliance on hardware-based isolation leads to heavy performance overhead, limiting their widespread adoption. Although constructing single-address-space microkernels based on safe language-based isolation is a promising approach to addressing the performance issue, this approach still faces challenges in maintaining the principle of minimality and enforcing capability-based, fine-grained access control over system resources. We propose safeL4, an approach to constructing microkernels based on safe languages. It guarantees minimality through low-level abstractions for unsafe operations, and implements a capability system based on the safe language's object capabilities to achieve fine-grained access control over all operations on system resources. We implement a prototype system in Rust, and our evaluation results show that the primitives provided by safeL4 are, on average, 1.9$\times$ faster than those of seL4.

Hardware Architecture 14
☆ An Embedded Ergonomic Posture Monitoring and AI-Assisted Home Learning System on a Raspberry Pi 3B Edge Platform
Truyen T. Le, Vinh Dang Ngoc, Thai Bao Huynh
During independent home study sessions, students frequently sustain improper sitting postures, accumulate excessive sedentary hours, and experience productivity loss from off-task digital distractions. Furthermore, learners often lack real-time pedagogical scaffolding for demanding self-study curricula. To mitigate these ergonomic and instructional challenges, this paper presents an affordable, privacy-preserving cyber-physical embedded system for domestic study spaces. Engineered on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B (1 GB RAM) paired with a UVC optical camera and a USB condenser microphone, the system executes on-device computer vision utilizing MediaPipe Pose and OpenCV to monitor upper-body alignment, sagittal head inclination, and coronal shoulder asymmetry in real time without persisting raw video streams. A deterministic finite state machine (FSM) quantifies active study durations, enforces health-compliant rest periods, and detects illicit smartphone usage. Simultaneously, an integrated multimodal AI tutoring agent parses voice and text queries via an encrypted API gateway, synthesizing Socratic conceptual hints rather than direct solutions. A lightweight parental web dashboard delivers encrypted session analytics and scheduling configurations. Empirical benchmarks on the physical prototype confirm an end-to-end inference latency of 244-250 ms at a 352x288 resolution (4.0-4.1 FPS), a trunk-angle estimation error of 4.39 degrees MAE over 5,760 synthetic ground-truth poses, a resident set size of 320 MB, a peak SoC temperature of 58.0 degrees Celsius under sustained load, and a 1.58 s total latency for the offline TTS feedback path, proving high practicality for resource-constrained edge deployment.
☆ A Differential Computing Accelerator for LLM Inference Leveraging Bit-Slice Transition Sparsity
Yifan Wang, Zetao Guo, You Xiao, Wendi Sun, Song Chen
Large language models (LLMs) have become foundational to modern artificial intelligence. Driven by scaling laws, their rapid growth poses increasing computational and memory challenges for deployment. To accelerate the general matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations that dominate LLM computation, bit-slice architectures decompose quantized operands along the bit dimension, exposing slice-level sparsity and redundancy. However, existing bit-slice designs primarily exploit sparsity in high-order slices, while dense low-order slices still offer substantial untapped reuse opportunities. We observe that bit-slice vectors (BSVs) are highly clustered in Hamming space, with many BSVs lying only a few bit flips away from a small set of representative patterns. Based on this observation, we propose ISTS, an algorithm-hardware co-designed accelerator that leverages representative BSV patterns as shared Steiner points to reuse partial sums across slices, substantially reducing computation. Specifically, the partial sum of each target BSV can be reconstructed from that of its assigned Steiner point using only a few additions or subtractions. On the algorithmic side, we propose Steiner Absorption Table Construction (SATC), which selects a compact set of Steiner points to absorb BSVs with only a few bidirectional bit flips, while FlipPrune selectively prunes flips to further expand the reusable BSV population. On the hardware side, we design a lightweight accelerator that supports Steiner reuse for static linear layer weights and runtime-generated attention K/V tensors. Comprehensive evaluations show that ISTS achieves average speedups of $3.09\times$, $2.41\times$, $2.18\times$, $1.27\times$, and $1.41\times$ over the state-of-the-art accelerators ANT, BBS, LUT Tensor Core, Transitive Array, and MCBP-BRCR, respectively.

☆ High-Throughput GPU Decoding of Quantum Bivariate Bicycle Codes under Circuit-Level Noise
Aditya Sodhani, Keshab K. Parhi
Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 $μ$s across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 $μ$s median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides $120\times$ higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at $p=0.002$, our proposed decoder achieves $7.58\times 10^{-6}$ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.
☆ DiversePlace: Diversity-Seeking Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Macro Placement
Wenrui Zhou, Jiashun Liu, Wenji Fang, Zhiyao Xie, Ling Pan
Macro placement is a critical early-stage decision in physical design because macro locations strongly constrain subsequent implementation stages. The task is difficult because these high-impact discrete decisions must be made before downstream quality can be measured accurately, forcing training to rely on fast but imperfect training-time oracles such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL). Existing RL-based placers therefore mostly optimize single HPWL-driven solutions, and their long sequential horizons often require heavy search assistance or offline expert data while leaving little room to preserve multiple competitive layouts. We address this gap by making quality-controlled diversity an explicit objective for macro placement. Instead of relying on a single proxy-optimal solution, we maintain a compact archive of HPWL-competitive yet meaningfully different placements for downstream selection. We realize this idea in DiversePlace, a curriculum proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that combines a quality-gated diversity reward with an expanding placement horizon, enabling from-scratch RL optimization while keeping exploration inside competitive HPWL regions. On the ISPD2005 benchmarks, DiversePlace consistently improves top-5, top-10, and top-20 archive diversity and achieves lower or virtually identical HPWL on all eight designs with better efficiency. Code: https://github.com/William030422/NIPS2026-DiversePlace.
☆ Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
Hoonki Lee, Haechan Shin, Hyuntaek Jung, Yeonu Choi, Sangyeob Kim
Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.

☆ MixMoMo: Accelerating Extra--Large MoE Inference with Mixed--Precision GPU--NPU Execution on Mobile Devices
Hailong Zou, Maoliang Li, Taohong Han, Haoze Chi, Zihao Zheng, Jiayu Chen, Xiang Chen
Mobile agents and on-device intelligence increasingly demand more capable models on smartphones. Through sparse expert activation, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity, yet growing numbers of fine-grained experts complicate loading and computation. Model compression complements expert offloading by reducing storage and computation costs. Among compression techniques, mixed-precision quantization assigns lower expert bitwidths to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, existing offline metrics and routing scores fail to reflect expert quantization sensitivity, undermining precision assignment. Diverse bitwidths also complicate balanced expert allocation across GPUs and NPUs with distinct execution characteristics, while tile-wise dequantization underutilizes NPU vector parallelism. We present MixMoMo, an efficient mixed-precision inference runtime for extra-large MoE models on heterogeneous mobile SoCs. MixMoMo combines offline quantization-impact profiles with activation-based runtime risk estimates for quality-constrained expert bitwidth assignment. It further adopts precision-structured execution for balanced GPU-NPU expert allocation and HVX-parallel dequantization for efficient NPU vector utilization. Across three MoE models and five benchmarks on two mobile platforms, MixMoMo achieves average decoding speedups of 3.72x over uniform Q4_0 and 1.53x over the strongest mixed-precision MoE baseline.
☆ Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
Musa Tur Farazi, Md Nasir Uddin, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.

☆ Algebraic Diversity of Switching Functions
Mitchell A. Thornton
Algebraic Diversity generalizes averaging over many observations to averaging one observation over a group of transformations matched to its structure. This paper develops the framework on the Boolean cube $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for the translations, the coordinate permutations, the hyperoctahedral group, and the general linear and affine groups. It determines the commutant of each action and gives closed forms for the group-averaged second-order statistic of one truth table, which collapses to the Walsh periodogram for the translations, to per-weight averages for the hyperoctahedral group, and to the weight up to complementation for the affine group. Bent functions are exactly those whose translation average is white, the Haar transform along an input order is the multiplexer tree of Shannon's expansion, and higher-order averages see only the weight below a first informative order, two for the translations and four for the affine group. A matched stabilizer stands in for repeated observations, since a vote over orbits of $s$ points divides by $s$ the number of noisy truth tables a target error requires. The same viewpoint gives the affine hull of a function as matched coordinates, an exact variance identity for XOR hashing, and matched hashes whose variance never exceeds that of a pairwise independent hash. Applications on public benchmarks include hash choice for approximate model counting, the decision of parity-structured formulas and the refutation of counting formulas modulo 3 and 4 from the spectra of clause blocks, separation of NPN classes by canonical spectra, tested on ISCAS-85 cut functions and all five-input classes, correction of noisy truth tables and protection of lookup tables by voting over symmetries, blind group matching, and an analog of the CLEAN algorithm that writes a truth table as the XOR of atoms in the fixed spaces of groups. All proofs are given in full.

☆ GPS: Guiding Phase-Level Prefetcher Selection with Data-Driven Method HPCA 2027
Buqing Xu, Mengming Li, Qijun Zhang, Ziyan Guo, Zhiyao Xie
Hardware prefetching is a widely used technique for hiding off-chip memory latency. Modern processors increasingly adopt composite prefetchers that combine multiple prefetching engines to handle the diverse memory access patterns found in real applications. However, coordinating multiple prefetchers requires a policy selection algorithm that maps observed system feedback to appropriate prefetching policies. Existing approaches suffer from two key limitations. First, relying on only a small set of features can lead to misleading prefetcher policies due to incomplete visibility into the system state. Second, limited on-chip hardware resources force these designs to use simple mapping mechanisms that cannot effectively navigate the large prefetching policy space. To address these challenges, we propose GPS, a data-driven framework for prefetcher selection that leverages comprehensive profiling and offline learning. GPS collects a rich set of features that capture both system behaviors and hardware resource states, and uses an offline machine learning model to learn the mapping between these features and the IPC-best policy. By offloading complex policy generation to software, GPS eliminates the need for costly online exploration and enables lightweight runtime execution through pre-generated policy hints. GPS reduces the performance gap to only 2.6%, compared to 13.6% and 14.2% in prior state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate GPS on SPEC CPU2006, SPEC CPU2017, and GAP benchmark suites. GPS outperforms the state-of-the-art prefetcher selection method I-POP by 12.14%, 8.34%, and 14.17% in geometric-mean IPC, respectively. GPS achieves these gains with only 778 bits of additional on-chip storage for runtime policy control.

☆ L2C2: Enhancing Large-scale Chiplets for Agent Long-Context LLM Inference with Sparse and Distributed Attention
Kangbo Bai, Zhonghua Mu, Hongze Zhou, Tianyu Jia
Long-context inference is a rising demand for LLMs, especially for agent applications. Sparse attention (SpAt) and chiplet technology are promising solutions to reduce computations and scale hardware performance. However, deploying SpAt on distributed chiplets necessitates context parallelism for workload partitioning, introducing complex distributed attention. In this work, we present L2C2, a system optimization for distributed SpAt in long-context inference. During the partial-prefill stage, we propose a novel Split-Comm Attention mechanism that leverages the high-bandwidth interconnect of chiplets to trade communication overhead for reduced memory access. We combine it with conventional Ring Attention to form a Bi-Mode method that adapts to varying input sequence lengths. During the decoding stage, we analyze the cause of memory access imbalance and address it by static interleaved token assignment. Dynamic agile cache balancing is also proposed to adapt to SpAt skewness. Evaluations show our optimization can achieve 1.45$\times$ and 1.53$\times$ speedup in partial-prefill and decoding with SpAt on large-scale chiplets.

☆ From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
Mehran Moghadam, Abu Masum, M. Hassan Najafi, Sercan Aygun, Di Wu
Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.
♻ ☆ Trading BRAM for LUTs: Hybrid Bit-Level Weight Storage for FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Networks DATE 2027
Dimitrios Sekertzis, Giorgos Dimitrakopoulos
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an attractive paradigm for energy-efficient AI inference, while their deployment on reconfigurable hardware enables application-specific acceleration without sacrificing model reprogrammability. However, realizing this potential on FPGAs is often severely constrained by the immense on-chip memory needed to store synaptic weights. Existing compression techniques reduce this storage requirement at the cost of weight precision or accuracy. This work presents a hybrid bit-level weight-storage scheme that trades BRAM capacity for FPGA logic resources while preserving the original weights unmodified. Selected weight bits are implemented using Look-Up Tables (LUTs), while the remaining bits are stored in BRAM and jointly reconstructed during inference. We integrate this approach into a spatial dataflow SNN architecture and introduce a practical bit-mapping heuristic that efficiently partitions weight bits between BRAM and LUT-based logic without modifying the weights. Experimental evaluation demonstrates more than 26% reduction in BRAM utilization with a modest increase in LUT and register usage, resulting in significant overall power savings.

♻ ☆ AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction
Pengju Liu, Nuo Xu, Winson Chen, Peijun Li, Yang, Zhao, Yu Cao, Caiwen Ding
Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
♻ ☆ Predictive Coding Implemented as a Hardware Substrate Computes Gradients faster than Backpropagation
Timothy Oh
Backpropagation has enabled modern deep learning but is difficult to realize as an online, fully distributed hardware system due to global error propagation, separate phases, and centralized memory. Predictive coding is an alternative learning algorithm with similar dynamics to backpropagation that arises from local prediction error dynamics. This paper shows that predictive coding can be instantiated as a discrete time digital hardware substrate, with local memory and computation, no instruction set architecture, and one physical core for each predictive-coding neuron. Each core stores its own activity and weights, communicates with the cores that it's connected to, and performs local gradient updates. By updating neuron cores concurrently, the architecture computes a network update in O(J+K) clock cycles. For dense layers of width n, this is O(n) cycles per update, compared with O(n^2) connection operations processed serially. This result is retained with scaling to larger predictive coding networks, demonstrating a decisive theoretical advantage for predictive coding instantiated in hardware.
Programming Languages 7
☆ An Efficient and Uniform CSP Solution Generator Generator
Ghiles Ziat, Martin Pépin
Constraint-based random testing is a powerful technique which aims at generating random test cases to verify functional properties of a program. Its objective is to determine whether a function satisfies a given property for every possible input. This approach requires firstly defining the property to satisfy, then secondly to provide a generator of inputs able to feed the program with the inputs generated. Besides, function inputs often need to satisfy certain constraints to ensure the function operates correctly, which makes the crafting of such a generator a hard task. In this paper, we are interested in the problem of manufacturing a uniform and efficient generator for the solutions of a CSP. In order to do that, we propose a specialized solving method that produces a well-suited representation for random sampling. Our solving method employs a dedicated propagation scheme based on the hypergraph representation of a CSP, and a custom split heuristic called birdge-first that emphasizes the interests of our propagation scheme. The generators we build are general enough to handle a wide range of use-cases. They are moreover uniform by construction, iterative and self-improving. We present a prototype built upon the AbSolute constraint solving library and demonstrate its performances on several realistic examples.

☆ SentryWard: Formal Verification of Warp-Specialized GPU Kernels
Mengdi Wu, Sreeram Vennam, Stephen Mell, Ziwei Zhou, Advay Kadam, Xinhao Cheng, Francois Costa, Alex Aiken, Oded Padon, Zhihao Jia
Modern GPU kernels overlap asynchronous data movement, computation on general-purpose cores (e.g., CUDA cores), and computation on specialized cores (e.g., tensor cores) using warp specialization. These asynchronous-overlap optimizations introduce complex synchronization requirements, where incorrect ordering of asynchronous operations can lead to data races, premature resource reuse, and incorrect results. Testing alone cannot guarantee correctness because such errors are nondeterministic and may only manifest in rare execution schedules, and existing GPU formal verification techniques have limited support for warp-specialized kernels. We present SentryWard, a framework for formally verifying warp-specialized GPU kernels. SentryWard integrates synchronization verification, data-race and resource-lifetime analysis, and functional equivalence checking. The key idea is to establish that synchronization induces the same ordering constraints across all possible execution schedules. SentryWard extends this well-synchronization analysis to modern GPU barriers with asynchronous transaction tracking and derives a schedule-independent happens-before graph. It then uses this graph to verify memory safety and construct symbolic output expressions for functional equivalence checking. While SentryWard generally assumes tensor shapes and kernel launch configurations are given and unrolls loops, it uses compact representations of repeated structures across threads and tensor computations to improve scalability. SentryWard is publicly available at https://github.com/gpu-verifier/sentryward.
♻ ☆ Denotational Results in Compiler Correctness and Comparisons with Operational Approaches
Jeremy G. Siek, Matthew Heimerdinger, Tianyu Chen, Darshal Shetty
Anyone setting out to prove a compiler correct must choose a style of semantics. The CakeML and CompCert projects, among others, show that operational semantics such as abstract machines and interpreters are viable choices. In this paper we explore whether denotational semantics can also be used in proofs of compiler correctness and evaluate the tradeoffs. We focus on a compiler from FPC, a language with lexically scoped functions and recursive types, to a first-order low-level intermediate language. This compiler includes closure conversion, but no prior proof of correctness with respect to denotational semantics covers closure conversion for a Turing-complete language. Compiler correctness requires that the denotation of a program be both preserved and reflected by the compiler. For closure conversion, reflection is the hard direction. We present the first denotational proofs of semantic reflection for closure conversion applied to a Turing-complete language, one proof with respect to a graph model and one with respect to Scott domains. For the graph-model proof we develop a new logical relation, the approximant logical relation, and for the Scott-domain proof we adapt a logical relation of Reynolds. As a first step in evaluating the tradeoffs, we compare mechanized correctness proofs of an eight-pass compiler, from FPC down to a typed low-level intermediate language, in five semantic styles. Two of the styles are denotational and three are operational. We find that no one semantics yields the shortest proofs for every compiler pass. We identify two factors that influence proof size. For operational semantics, proof size tends to grow with how much the runs of the source and target differ. For denotational semantics, the proofs are succinct when the correctness of a pass is an equation between meanings, and lengthy when a pass needs a logical relation.

♻ ☆ Increasing the Precision of IR Mapping for Incremental Data Flow Analysis
Anushri Jana, Kush Goradiya, Uday P Khedker
Static analysis tools operate on an Intermediate Representation (IR) --- an internal model of the program on which dataflow analysis computes and stores facts against IR object identifiers. Incremental dataflow analysis reuses these cached facts across consecutive program versions, but requires an accurate mapping between IR objects in the old and new versions. When this mapping is imprecise, the consequence is not merely a missed optimization: unmapped IR objects inflate the change set, increasing the number of program points that the analyzer must recompute and forcing it to redo work that a more precise mapping would have avoided. This cost is not specific to any one kind of IR object; it arises wherever IR-level identity is unstable across versions. Any IR that decomposes nested source expressions generates temporary variables which are assigned names by a method-local counter that shifts whenever a statement is inserted or deleted earlier in the method, breaking any name- or attribute-based mapping. We present a systematic algorithm that establishes a sound, oneto-one mapping of these temporary variables across consecutive versions, and formalize and prove the soundness of the mapping, guaranteeing that every produced mapping is semantically correct. The resulting precise mapping shrinks the change set, reducing the number of program points the incremental analysis must recompute. Implemented within the Soot framework for Jimple IR and evaluated on 8 real-world Java projects with genuine edits from the BUGSWARM dataset, our approach reduces the IR change set by over 82% on average compared to Reviser's graph-differencing algorithm, while completing the full pipeline within 250 ms per project---directly countering the common assumption that a more precise change set necessarily costs more time to compute.
♻ ☆ VirtualSet: Receiver-Indexed Authority Compilation for Query-to-Action Continuity in Executable Ontologies
Qunhui Zhang
An ontology edit can preserve a query answer while replacing the evidence that justified an action on it. We study when the original approval remains valid. VirtualSet compiles the evaluated query and a trusted grant into a single-use capability. The query result fixes the approved objects; policy grants actions on their type. Each field or link is recorded under its owning receiver type. For conjunctive filters over stable, single-valued relations, preserving the observed paths and target rows suffices for current target membership at batch entry. In 32 Java cases requiring recorded evidence, finite paths admitted 24 continuations versus 16 for a type-level closure. We then issued approvals before controlled changes in procurement and laboratory ontologies and presented the original credentials afterward. In all 40 scenarios, the post-change selections returned the same object identifiers as at issuance. With the same Java authorization layer, typed navigation and SQL over a stable view each retained 22 original approvals and blocked 18. Retargeting the second relation invalidated approvals that traversed it while preserving those based only on the first. By tracing the receiver type at each access in a validated query, VirtualSet distinguishes approvals for the same objects according to the evidence each approval depends on.

♻ ☆ Generic Constraints Projection: An Exact Criterion for Preserving Type Comparison Reports under Record Width Extension
Qunhui Zhang
A release can preserve a program's type and output while changing a comparison cited in an approved report. A publisher needs to know whether the original approval covers the new release's report under the same identifier and which source comparisons yield different reports. Reconstruction answers these questions after projection. We study them in Generic Constraints Projection for a pure record language whose comparison stops at type equality. For a fixed source export over ground types built from immutable records, primitives, top and bottom, we prove an exact criterion under record width extension. Two independently projected valid certificates yield the same report up to session renaming exactly when their read bindings agree and the actual type at each old stopping position is unchanged. With read bindings fixed, we trace these positions to input paths. If each old record admits a fresh field name, the resulting subtree equalities form the unique irredundant conjunction on old input-record paths for whole-report preservation. For completed mixed edits, a separate criterion uses the new valid certificate to check required types, old leaf endpoints and the surplus fields that keep old branches open. Across two consecutive API Extractor release windows, one published member addition changed an interface yet preserved both comparisons in our mapper. Given the old export, input types and fixed read bindings, occurrence-specific paths identify, before reprojection, exactly which source comparisons would yield different reports after proposed field additions.

♻ ☆ safeL4: Rethinking Safe-Language-Based Single Address Space Microkernels ASPLOS 2027
Zheyuan Xu, Xiaobei Zhang, Zihan Li, Zekai Nie, Guangtao Zhu, Zhuang Lu, Qianying Zhang, Shijun Zhao, Haibo Chen, Rui Hou
Microkernels provide good features such as high security, safety, and flexibility, but their reliance on hardware-based isolation leads to heavy performance overhead, limiting their widespread adoption. Although constructing single-address-space microkernels based on safe language-based isolation is a promising approach to addressing the performance issue, this approach still faces challenges in maintaining the principle of minimality and enforcing capability-based, fine-grained access control over system resources. We propose safeL4, an approach to constructing microkernels based on safe languages. It guarantees minimality through low-level abstractions for unsafe operations, and implements a capability system based on the safe language's object capabilities to achieve fine-grained access control over all operations on system resources. We implement a prototype system in Rust, and our evaluation results show that the primitives provided by safeL4 are, on average, 1.9$\times$ faster than those of seL4.
comment: Accepted to the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS 2027)
Data Structures and Algorithms 31
☆ Linear Single-Source Shortest Path, Almost
Iman Gholami, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
We give a comparison-addition algorithm for single-source shortest paths in undirected graphs with nonnegative real edge lengths. For each input with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, its expected running time is $O(m+n\log\log\log n)$. It terminates almost surely. Every terminating run returns exact distances and a shortest-path tree on the reachable vertices. The bound is independent of the ratio of edge lengths and is linear whenever $m=Ω(n\log\log\log n)$.
☆ Robust large-scale approximate solutions of the constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem
Xuan Kien Phung, Sylvie Hamel
The Kemeny aggregation ranking problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the well-known Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy many fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall-tau distance which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. While having various applications in computational social choice, machine learning, operations research, and biology, the problem of computing the consensus rankings is NP-hard and encounters a severe bottleneck in practice. In this paper, we consider the more general Kemeny aggregation ranking problem under immutable input pairwise constraints and propose robust and scalable approximate methods with provable guarantees. We thus provide an algorithmic solution to the more general constrained problem of incorporating a posteriori immutable pairwise constraints into past rankings (e.g., historical voter ballots or legacy laboratory assays) without incurring the cost of generating new data. Our base algorithm $Γ$-XCC provides a source of rankings with a bounded constant approximation factor. $Γ$-XCC generalizes the Copeland ranking method and satisfies the constrained Condorcet consistency property, an extension of the Condorcet winner criterion for elections with immutable pairwise constraints. Thereby, our methods provide large-scale solutions that address the reliability and explainability issues. Our algorithms are also applicable to weighted tournaments with input pairwise constraints and satisfy similar properties in this larger context.
☆ Pinwheel Scheduling is PSPACE-Complete
Dimitris Fotakis, Sotiris Kanellopoulos, Giorgos Mitropoulos, Aris Pagourtzis, Christos Papadimitriou, Christos Pergaminelis, Thanos Tolias
Pinwheel Scheduling is a classical periodic scheduling problem, receiving as input the deadlines $d_i$ of $n$ tasks and asking for an infinite schedule with one task per time unit, such that every task $i$ is scheduled at least once in every $d_i$ time units. Holte, Mok, Rosier, Tulchinsky, and Varvel introduced the problem in 1989 and showed that it lies in \(\PSPACE\). Its exact complexity has been open since then. \(\NP\)-hardness for explicitly listed deadlines was established only recently, and membership in \(\NP\) is open. In this work we prove that Pinwheel Scheduling is \(\PSPACE\)-complete when the deadlines are written in binary. This finally settles the long-standing open question about the complexity of Pinwheel Scheduling. We present a chain of reductions, starting from Periodic 3-SAT, a classical \(\PSPACE\)-complete problem, and using two newly-defined intermediate periodic scheduling problems. These intermediate problems can be seen as periodically assigning tasks to days, with each day containing a fixed number of slots (\emph{hours}) in which tasks are scheduled. In the first of these problems, each day is additionally allowed to contain \emph{breaks}, that is, hours in which no task can be scheduled.
☆ Monotone Crossing Lattices for Exact Binary Optimization Encodings on Rydberg Arrays
Liyin Hu, Shengminjie Chen, Ran Miao, Zhiyi Huang, Xiaohan Shan, Jialin Zhang, Xiaoming Sun
Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays realize maximum-weight independent set encoding on unit-disk graphs under the ideal blockade model, but embedding nonlocal interactions requires auxiliary atoms and limits the size of tractable instances. We introduce a four-state unit-disk crossing cell that couples directly to adjacent cells, with interfaces enforcing one-sided propagation: along occupied paths directed away from the diagonal, copy bits are nondecreasing. For the maximum-weight independent set problem, uniform cell weights guarantee that every ground state of the encoded instance decodes to an optimal solution of the original problem, even when local copies disagree. For binary quadratic objectives subject to pairwise Boolean constraints, every feasible optimum yields consistent active copies and a target weight given by an explicit constant offset minus the source objective. A rectangular variant of the architecture further encodes minimum set cover problem. Prior to constraint-induced site deletions, the full layout requires $2n^2 - n$ sites, halving the leading-order site count of a fixed complete-grid reference, while activity pruning yields an exact site count set by the propagation span. Across 18 paired benchmarks with independent ordering from a shared candidate pool, the layout reduces site counts by 12.1%-54.0%.

☆ Min-Plus Products and Dynamic Programming with Few Violations of the Adjacent Monge Inequalities
Yanqiao Chen
Local rewards can introduce negative adjacent mixed differences into a convex transition cost. If a cost array $B$ has $s(B)$ such differences, we express it as a Monge array minus $s(B)$ weighted rectangles and sweep its columns, maintaining the lower envelope of the active rows. For explicit finite $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ and $L=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$, we compute $A\otimes B$ and the smallest minimizing index for every entry in $\mathcal{O}(n^2L+ns(B)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ space, giving near-quadratic time for arbitrary $A$ when $s(B)=\mathcal{O}(n)$, including right factors with $Θ(n^2)$ positive differences. For block costs given by a constant-time Monge oracle and $r$ signed rectangle corrections, the sweep activates each row when its prefix optimum becomes available and computes an optimal contiguous partition in $\mathcal{O}((n+r)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n+r)$ working space. The sweep handles convex transitions with interval rules and assigns one rectangle to each internal edge or hyperedge reward in a convex block cost, giving near-linear exact algorithms on sparse inputs for ordered graph modularity, weighted contiguous cluster editing, all-or-nothing HyperLam, and bounded-rank strict hypergraph modularity. Let $c_{\mathrm{APSP}}$ denote the deterministic exponent of all-pairs shortest paths with polynomially bounded integer weights. For fixed $3-c_{\mathrm{APSP}}<α\le1$, any deterministic $\mathcal{O}(n^β)$-time min-plus product algorithm for polynomially bounded integer matrices with $s(B)\le n^{1+α}$ satisfies $β\ge c_{\mathrm{APSP}}-1+α$. The reduction from general integer min-plus multiplication uses right factors obtained from $(j-k)^2$ by at most $n^{1+α}$ interval discounts, with $Θ(n^2)$ positive differences and all remaining differences negative.
☆ Low-degree hardness rules out eigenvalue tests but not eigenvector tests
Xuan Chen, Shuangping Li
We study what low-degree hardness implies for spectral tests, with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE) as the null distribution. We show that, once a fixed amount of Gaussian noise is added, it rules out every test based on eigenvalues, but not tests based on eigenvectors. For eigenvalues, if the low-degree advantage vanishes at logarithmic degree, then the joint law of the noisy eigenvalues converges to that of the GOE in total variation. For eigenvectors, we construct planted distributions with vanishing low-degree advantage whose eigenvalues follow the GOE law exactly at every noise level, yet whose noisy eigenvectors still distinguish them from the GOE. A single eigenvector can suffice. After a small amount of noise, a polynomial-time test that uses only the span of a fixed fraction of the top eigenvectors also succeeds, even when the low-degree advantage vanishes at a prescribed polylogarithmic degree. To prove the eigenvalue result, we split the noise into three increments. The first uses the low-degree assumption to establish eigenvalue rigidity. The second couples the two spectra through Dyson Brownian motion and applies homogenization to obtain a transport estimate. The third uses Gaussian smoothing to convert this estimate into closeness in total variation.
comment: 65 pages, 4 figures
☆ Toward a human-friendly proof of a polynomial bound for the Directed Grid Theorem
Victor Campos, Allen Ibiapina, Raul Lopes, Rodrigo Nogueira, Ignasi Sau
The Directed Grid Theorem of Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC 2015] states that there is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of directed treewidth at least $f(k)$ contains a cylindrical grid of order $k$ as a butterfly minor. Their function is not elementary, and Hatzel, Kreutzer, Garlet Milani, and Muzi [FOCS 2024] improved it to a tower of exponentials of height $22$, by a proof in three stages through paths and cycles of well-linked sets. In this paper we prove each stage with a polynomial bound, so that $f$ can be chosen to be a polynomial of degree $20\,031\,568$. As a consequence, Younger's conjecture, proved by Reed, Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas [Combinatorica, 1996], holds with a polynomial bound: for the polynomial $f$ that we construct, every digraph without $k$ pairwise disjoint cycles has a feedback vertex set of size at most $(k-1)f(k)$. In fact, beyond cycles, we obtain polynomial packing-covering bounds for every strongly connected digraph that is a butterfly minor of a cylindrical grid.
☆ Uniform Guarded Bootstrapping for Topology-Sensitive Directed Shortest Paths STOC 2027
Bin Cai
On a source star, every leaf distance is an input weight. Thus computing labeled distances need not reveal their order. For a rooted directed topology, let $K$ be the least worst-case sum of comparisons and additions among finite deterministic programs specialized to that topology and correct for every nonnegative weighting. We give one deterministic program that takes the graph as input. This graph-input-uniform algorithm has total comparison-addition RAM time $O(m+n+KΦ(K)\exp(O(\log_2^*(K+2))))$, where $n$ and $m$ count vertices and arcs, and $Φ$ is a regularized product of successive logarithms. An active core is the small graph remaining after directly recoverable distances are separated. The algorithm chooses its parameters from the core size. Frozen entry ceilings let each interrupted local call be replayed on a small completion, whose complete-run bound controls the stopped work. The cost coefficient satisfies a linear one-step recurrence, yielding at most exponential growth in the number of generations. This permits a depth chosen from the measured core size. For $m=O(n)$, the solver gives $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4+o(1)})$ time, improving the sparse directed bound of Duan, Mao, Shu, and Yin. A complementary result uses reusable dominator calibration for changing seed vectors on a fixed weighted graph.

An earlier version was publicly posted as STOC 2027 submission #1592 on 2 November 2026 at 11:59 pm AoE (3 November 2026, 7:59 pm Asia/Shanghai): https://sigact-stoc.github.io/stoc2027/. This arXiv version updates the related-work discussion to cite arXiv:2611.26453v2. It builds on the resource framework and active-core reduction in arXiv:2609.04825v1
☆ Square-root comparison, Turnpike, and exact semidefinite feasibility
C. S. Elder
Given positive integers $a_i,K$, put $S=\sum_{i=1}^k\sqrt{a_i}$. We construct a realizable Turnpike instance in which the minimum spacing of distinct distances and the smallest nonzero addition residual are both at most $|S-K|$ when $S\ne K$. With approximation oracles, one three-distance realizability query decides $S\le K$. For unordered lists of radical sums with nonnegative rational coefficients, a polynomial-time substitution by integers preserves every normalized ruler. We give the classical reduction of square-root comparison to exact semidefinite feasibility in both threshold directions. The comparison enters through numerical separation and marked sorting; the integer recoding needs no such comparison for unordered reconstruction.

☆ Parameterized Algorithms for Minimum Sum Vertex Cover on Dense Graphs
Shubhada Aute, Noleen Köhler, Fahad Panolan
The \textsc{Minimum Sum Vertex Cover} (MSVC) problem asks for a linear ordering of the vertices of a graph that minimizes the sum, over all edges, of the position of the earlier endpoint. We study its parameterized complexity on graphs that become a clique, cluster graph, or a split graph after deleting a small set of vertices, called the Modulator. We prove that MSVC is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized jointly by the cluster modulator size and the maximum clique size in the remaining cluster graph, while allowing arbitrarily many cliques. For the clique modulator parameterization, we present a combinatorial algorithm that avoids the integer quadratic programming used in prior work [Aute, Panolan, Theoretical Computer Science, 2025]. We also introduce a vertex-weighted formulation of MSVC and obtain an XP algorithm parameterized by the clique modulator size. Using this algorithm as a subroutine, we develop an XP algorithm parameterized by the split modulator size. These results extend the known structural parameterizations of MSVC and highlight weighted MSVC as a promising direction for further research.
comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)
☆ Prophet Inequalities for Mixtures of I.I.D. Random Variables
Felix Fischer, Kevin Schewior
A latent index $J\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ is drawn from a prior $π$. Conditional on $J=j$, a gambler observes random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ drawn independently from a non-negative component distribution $F_j$. The gambler knows $n$, the prior $π$, and the component distributions $F_1,\ldots,F_k$, but not $J$, observes the values sequentially, and selects at most one value at the time it is revealed. We show that the largest $α$ such that the gambler can guarantee to select a value of $α\cdot\mathbb{E}[\max_iX_i]$ in expectation, for all distributions where this expectation is finite, is \[ α=\frac1e+\frac{1}{k^{2/3+o(1)}}. \] The lower bound is achieved by the better of two variants of the standard secretary rule. The upper bound uses a finely tuned instance of the common-scale model, which scales a sequence of independent random variables by a single latent variable.
☆ A Local-Counting Approach for Distributed Induced Path Detection
Keren Censor-Hillel, Julian Ewaied
A well-known application of the celebrated color-coding technique is fast detection of paths in a distributed setting with limited bandwidth, by propagating a signal along colorful paths [Even et al., DISC 2017]. However, since vertices of the same color are indistinguishable by this procedure, it cannot detect induced paths, as they appear the same as cycles. We make the following observation. If, for a given edge, we \emph{count} the number of such signals over all permutations of the random coloring that terminate at that edge, then we can separate an induced path from a cycle: an induced path contributes one to that count, while a cycle contributes two. Refining and generalizing this observation gives our \emph{local-counting approach}, which allows us to separate induced paths from any other subgraph. We establish the following end results, all improving upon the state of the art in their round complexities and refined detection variants. * An $O(1)$-round algorithm for induced $P_4$ detection. * $O(Δ)$-round algorithms for detection of induced $P_5$ and $P_6$. * An $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})$-round algorithm for detection of induced $P_5$ in induced-$C_4$ free graphs.
☆ Tropical and maximum colorful matchings in vertex-colored graphs
Johanne Cohen, Yannis Manoussakis, Hong Phong Pham, Zsolt Tuza
A subgraph of a vertex-colored graph istropical if it contains every color. We study matchings by the number of colors they cover. A matching is maximum colorful if no matching covers more colors. When a tropical matching exists, the maximum colorful matchings are exactly the tropical matchings. We give polynomial-time algorithms for two problems: a maximum matching that covers the most colors, and a tropical matching with the fewest edges. Both algorithms rest on a counterpart of Berge's theorem: a matching is optimal if and only if it admits no tropical augmentation, or no tropical reduction. These are chains of alternating paths linked by relays, and each one is found by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph. The same tools give a maximum colorful matching with the fewest edges, and show that all maximum matchings that are maximum colorful are connected by flips. Finally, the sets of colors that a matching can cover form a matroid. The greedy algorithm then computes a matching of maximum color weight. This paper extends the conference version and the PhD thesis of one of the authors.
☆ Concavity of cardinality-constrained interval stabbing and interval cover problems
Janez Brank, Tomaž Hočevar
We consider the cardinality-constrained interval stabbing problem, in which the goal is to maximize the total weight of intervals hit by at least one of at most $k$ selected points. Although this problem does not admit a simple greedy solution, we show that its optimal value is a concave function of $k$. We establish this result using a linear programming formulation whose relaxation always admits an optimal solution with integer values. This allows us to prove concavity for the original problem. We further extend the result to the related interval cover problem. These concavity properties provide a basis for applying Lagrangian optimization using algorithms for the corresponding unconstrained problems.
☆ Near-Tight Robust Coresets for Clustering in Euclidean Spaces
Pengsen Huang, Yi Li, Xuan Wu
This paper considers coresets for the robust $(k,z)$-clustering problem with $m$ outliers in Euclidean spaces. A robust coreset is a weighted subset of the data that, for every set of $k$ centers and every outlier budget $0\leq b\leq m$, approximates the clustering cost with $b$ outliers removed to within relative error $ε$. For every constant $z\geq 1$, we prove that the optimal worst-case size of such coresets over all ambient dimensions is \[ Θ(m) + \widetildeΘ_z(\min\{kε^{-(z+2)}, k^{2(z+1)/(z+2)}ε^{-2} + km^{z/(z+2)}ε^{-4/(z+2)}\}), \qquad 1\leq z \leq 2, \] \[ Θ(m) + \widetildeΘ_z(\min\{kε^{-(z+2)}, k^{2(z+1)/(z+2)}ε^{-2} + k \min\{m, \sqrt{m}ε^{-z/2}\} \}), \qquad z > 2. \]
☆ Directed $k$-Disjoint Shortest Paths in Polynomial Time
Yang Cao, Haoran Qi, Hanzhi Wang
The $k$-Disjoint Shortest Paths problem asks for pairwise vertex-disjoint shortest paths connecting $k$ prescribed terminal pairs in a graph with positive edge weights. Eilam-Tzoreff [DAM 1998] asked whether it is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed $k$. Lochet [SODA 2021] answered this for undirected graphs, while for directed graphs it has remained open for every $k\ge3$. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for directed graphs and every fixed $k$, resolving this open problem for all graphs.
☆ Almost Tight Hardness of Approximation for $0$-Extension
Qingyun Chen, Weihao Zhu
In the $0$-Extension problem, we are given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with non-negative edge weights $w: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, a collection $T \subseteq V$ of $k$ terminals, and a metric $D$ over terminals $T$. The goal is to find a retraction $f:V\rightarrow T$ that maps every terminal to itself, while minimizing the sum over all edges of the product of the edge's weight and the distance in $D$ between the terminals to which its endpoints are assigned, i.e., \[ \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E} w_{\{u,v\}} \cdot D(f(u), f(v)). \] Fakcharoenphol, Harrelson, Rao, and Talwar achieve the best known approximation ratio of $O(\log k / \log \log k)$, while the known approximation hardness is $Ω(\sqrt{\log k})$ assuming the unique games conjecture. In this work, we establish an $Ω(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ hardness of approximation for every constant $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and arbitrarily large fixed $k$, almost matching the upper bound in the exponent of $\log k$. The main technical contribution is an $Ω(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation. Our construction is inspired by randomized extensions of expanders introduced by Schwartz and Tur for the metric relaxation. The result then follows from an existing theorem by Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz that translates the integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation to the approximation hardness for every fixed $k$.
☆ A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for ARRIVAL
Chenglin Fan, Jeonseong Kim
In ARRIVAL, a token moves through a directed graph from a specified starting vertex, alternating between the two outgoing arcs of each vertex on successive departures. The problem asks whether the token ever reaches a given destination. Although the walk can be exponentially long, we give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, resolving an open problem. We first average the local routing rules and then restore the original rules on selected periods. The number of refinement rounds is at most the number of nonterminal vertices. The algorithm extends to explicitly given cyclic successor lists. It also computes exact departure counts when every nonterminal vertex has a path to an absorbing terminal and recovers the configuration of the walk at any binary-encoded time.

☆ Toggle Tree: A New Data Structure for Efficient Parallel Graph Processing PPoPP 2027
Xinjian Jiang, Youzhe Liu, Yan Gu, Yihan Sun
We present the Toggle Tree, a parallel data structure for frontier-based graph algorithms. A Toggle Tree is used to represent a subset of vertices using hierarchical bit vectors, enabling efficient parallel updates, traversal, and set-wise reductions without global packing. It provides an IndexSet interface that unifies a wide range of parallel graph algorithms under a common abstraction of frontiers and active sets, and an IndexMap interface that also incorporates priority-queue semantics. Specifically, the Toggle Tree aims to combine the advantages of traditional sparse and dense frontier representations, offering both provable theoretical guarantees and high efficiency in practice. Using Toggle Trees, we implement five fundamental graph algorithms, including breadth-first search (BFS), k-core, degree-based graph coloring, single-source shortest paths using Bellman-Ford, and weighted-BFS (wBFS). Across a diverse set of large real-world graphs and the five graph problems, our implementations outperform state-of-the-art baselines, including GBBS and PASGAL, achieving substantial speedups. Our code is publicly available.

☆ Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
Masayuki Miyamoto
The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound. In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.
☆ SAT-Driven Exact Treewidth via Safe Separators and Structure-Aware Encodings
Yannik Krone
Treewidth is a standard measure of graph structure, but computing it exactly is NP-hard. SAT- and MaxSAT-based approaches provide a uniform way to solve treewidth by encoding it in conjunctive normal form and delegating the search to modern Boolean solvers, thus directly benefiting from continued progress in SAT technology. This report studies how to strengthen such SAT-driven solvers with structural reasoning and low-overhead guidance, both at the meta-algorithmic level and within the encoding itself. Starting from a baseline SAT/MaxSAT formulation, we investigate structure-based simplifications that reduce solver effort while preserving exactness, and we evaluate practical heuristic enhancements (fast upper/lower bounds and solver guidance) within iterative SAT and MaxSAT workflows. Experiments show consistent speedups on instances with exploitable structure, and clarify where SAT-based approaches remain limited.

☆ Online Network Design with Batch Processing
Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu
An online service chooses which waiting jobs to start together. Each finishes after its own processing time, and the longest determines the next possible launch. We charge network cost plus either total flow or the sum of per-batch maximum flows. For TCP acknowledgment with a fixed fee per launch, the optimal deterministic total-flow ratio is \(1+ρ\), where \(ρ\) is the processing-time spread. For batch maxima, a union of intervals on the release-time axis gives the exact offline cost when batches may overlap. It yields an offline \(2\)-approximation and pays for an online timer of ratio five. The optimal deterministic ratio is two at equal lengths and lies in \([2+2\sqrt2,5]\) at unrestricted spread. How often can later batches incur the same blocking delay? Rooted purchases can be combined, giving a polynomial-time \(3+2\sqrt2\) guarantee for batch maxima on undirected Steiner networks. A mobile server can concatenate walks in order, transferring an instantaneous maximum-wait ratio \(α\) to a batch-maximum flow ratio \(3α+6\). With \(k\) ephemeral facilities sharing one processor and one site per launch, separate openings can each incur the wait. The optimal deterministic batch-maximum ratio is then \(Θ(k)\) at unrestricted spread. The upper bound uses exact assignments, computable in polynomial time for fixed \(k\).
☆ Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
Ishaq Aden-Ali, Adam Sealfon, Adam Smith, Thomas Steinke, Jonathan Ullman
Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

♻ ☆ Parameterized Complexity of Finding a Maximum Common Vertex Subgraph Without Isolated Vertices
Palash Dey, Anubhav Dhar, Ashlesha Hota, Sudeshna Kolay, Aritra Mitra
In this paper, we study the Maximum Common Vertex Subgraph problem: Given two input graphs $G_1,G_2$ and a non-negative integer $h$, is there a common subgraph $H$ on at least $h$ vertices such that there is no isolated vertex in $H$. In other words, each connected component of $H$ has at least $2$ vertices. This problem naturally arises in graph theory along with other variants of the well-studied Maximum Common Subgraph problem and also has applications in computational social choice. We show that this problem is NP-hard and provide an FPT algorithm when parameterized by $h$. Next, we conduct a study of the problem on common structural parameters like vertex cover number, maximum degree, treedepth, pathwidth and treewidth of one or both input graphs. We derive a complete dichotomy of parameterized results for our problem with respect to individual parameterizations as well as combinations of parameterizations from the above structural parameters. This provides us with a deep insight into the complexity theoretic and parameterized landscape of this problem.

♻ ☆ On the Assadi Liu Tarjan Auction Algorithm for Bipartite Matching: Simplification, Alternative Analysis, and Hard Instance
Christian Konrad, Kheeran K. Naidu, Archie Walton, Yiquan Wang
Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan [SOSA'21] gave an auction algorithm that outputs a $(1-ε)$-approximation to Maximum Matching in bipartite graphs. Their algorithm computes a sequence of $O(\frac{1}{ε^2})$ maximal matchings in subgraphs of the input graph and can be implemented in the multi-pass streaming setting with $O(\frac{1}{ε^2})$ passes in a straightforward manner, which constitutes the state-of-the-art pass/approximation trade-off result in the multi-pass streaming setting. Their analysis uses tools from combinatorial auctions and, at its heart, relies on a clever potential function argument. Their proof, however, provides only limited insight into the inner workings of the algorithm. In this paper, we revisit the ALT-algorithm and present the following contributions. Simplification: The ALT-algorithm is built upon a freezing mechanism where vertices on one side of the bipartition that have already been rematched $Θ(\frac{1}ε)$ times over the course of the algorithm remain matched to their current partner forever. We show that this mechanism is in fact unnecessary, i.e., no special treatment of such vertices is needed. Alternative Analysis: We give an alternative analysis of the algorithm that is based on augmenting paths. Our analysis allows for a reinterpretation as one that follows the traditional approach of searching for and eliminating augmenting paths. Our analysis also copes with the removal of the freezing mechanism in a natural way, whereas the analysis of Assadi et al. strictly depends on its use. Hard Instance: We provide the first hard instance on which the algorithm requires $Ω(\frac{1}{ε^2})$ iterations/maximal matching computations. The instance is a simple path graph, where we exhibit a cyclic behaviour that prevents fast progress.

♻ ☆ Testing Expansion without Connectivity via Return Probabilities
Nikolas Melissaris
We study whether every connected component of a bounded-degree graph is an edge expander, given access to its neighbor lists. Dinur and Goldreich give a tester using $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)n^α$ queries for every fixed $α>2/3$. We obtain \[ \widetilde O_{d,c,β}\!\left(\frac{n^{1/2+β}}{\varepsilon} +\frac{\sqrt n}{\varepsilon^4}\right) \] queries for every fixed $0<β\le1$. The tester accepts graphs whose components have edge expansion at least $c$ and rejects graphs $\varepsilon$-far from having edge expansion at least $κβc^2/d$ in every component (for an absolute constant $κ>0$), each with probability at least $2/3$. No structural promise is imposed on the input. The tester compares pairwise collision probabilities at two walk lengths and starts further walks at vertices where sampled endpoints coincide. These additional samples control the contribution of vertices with larger return probabilities. We show that the resulting conditions force the longer walk to be nearly uniform on an induced expander with few edges leaving it. For fixed degree $d\ge3$ and completeness threshold $0
♻ ☆ Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
Han Zhong, Yinyu Ye
We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out polynomial-time complexity of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a "price" of algorithmic anarchy.
♻ ☆ Undirected Multiple-Unicast Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu
In undirected multiple-unicast networks, where independent messages are sent between specified source-destination pairs, network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas fractional routing splits and forwards individual messages along paths without mixing them. Proposed in 2004 by Li and Li and independently by Harvey, Kleinberg, and Lehman, the multiple-unicast conjecture---long a central open problem in network coding with deep connections to computational complexity---asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same achievable rate region. We construct a counterexample refuting this conjecture and use it to reduce block transfers in external-memory data rearrangement, thereby accelerating external-memory integer sorting and answering in the affirmative the longstanding question of Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) on whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound. Specifically, we give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $Θ(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $$O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right),$$ where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. This bound asymptotically improves on the classical $Θ\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log(N/M)}{\log(M/B)}\right]\right)$ comparison-sorting bound in certain parameter regimes. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean 4. Our reduction is independent of the address-field interchange construction. Using the one from recent work on multitape integer multiplication gives the bound for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, with an $\varepsilon$-dependent constant.

♻ ☆ Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
Tingwei Hu, Lili Mei, Guochuan Zhang
We study the allocation of indivisible goods to agents with budgets and additive valuations. Each agent compares its bundle with every budget-feasible subset of another agent's bundle or of the unallocated goods. We give a strongly polynomial algorithm for computing an allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1), even when agents have different valuations and budgets. Deciding whether a given allocation satisfies EF1 is coNP-complete. Equivalently, deciding whether it violates EF1 is NP-complete. When all agents have the same valuation, we can compute an EF1 allocation with welfare at least $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ times the maximum feasible welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, for any $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Finding an allocation that is envy-free up to any good (EFX) is NP-hard even for one agent. We give polynomial-time EFX algorithms when each agent values goods in proportion to their sizes or when the number of distinct positive item values per agent is bounded by a constant.

♻ ☆ Space Complexity Dichotomies for Subgraph Finding Problems in the Streaming Model
Yu-Sheng Shih, Meng-Tsung Tsai, Yen-Chu Tsai, Ying-Sian Wu
We study the space complexity of four variants of the standard subgraph finding problem in the streaming model. Specifically, given an $n$-vertex input graph and a fixed pattern graph on at least three vertices, we consider two settings: undirected simple graphs, denoted by $G$ and $H$, and oriented graphs, denoted by $\vec{G}$ and $\vec{H}$. Depending on the setting, the task is to decide whether $G$ contains $H$ as a subgraph or as an induced subgraph, or whether $\vec{G}$ contains $\vec{H}$ as a subgraph or as an induced subgraph. Let $\textsc{Sub}(H)$, $\textsc{IndSub}(H)$, $\textsc{Sub}(\vec{H})$, and $\textsc{IndSub}(\vec{H})$ denote these four variants, respectively. An oriented graph is well-oriented if it admits a bipartition in which every arc is oriented from the same part to the other, and a vertex is internal if both its in-degree and out-degree are non-zero. For each variant, we obtain a complete dichotomy theorem, briefly summarized as follows. \begin{itemize} \item $\textsc{Sub}(H)$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-Ω(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if $H$ is bipartite. \item $\textsc{IndSub}(H)$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-Ω(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if $H$ is $P_3$, $P_4$, or $\mbox{co-}P_3$. \item $\textsc{Sub}(\vec{H})$ can be solved by a deterministic single-pass $n^{2-Ω(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if every connected component of $\vec H$ is either a well-oriented bipartite graph or a tree containing at most one internal vertex. \item $\textsc{IndSub}(\vec{H})$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-Ω(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if the underlying undirected simple graph $H$ is a $\mbox{co-}P_3$. \end{itemize} All our upper bounds are attained by deterministic algorithms that find a copy, whereas all our lower bounds hold even for randomized algorithms that only detect one.S

♻ ☆ Dynamic Tensor Product Regression NeurIPS 2022
Aravind Reddy, Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang
In this work, we initiate the study of Dynamic Tensor Product Regression. One has matrices $A_1\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times d_1},\ldots,A_q\in \mathbb{R}^{n_q\times d_q}$ and a label vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\ldots n_q}$, and the goal is to solve the regression problem with the design matrix $A$ being the tensor product of the matrices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_q$ i.e. $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\ldots d_q}} \|(A_1\otimes \ldots\otimes A_q)x-b\|_2$. At each time step, one matrix $A_i$ receives a sparse change, and the goal is to maintain a sketch of the tensor product $A_1\otimes\ldots \otimes A_q$ so that the regression solution can be updated quickly. Recomputing the solution from scratch for each round is very slow and so it is important to develop algorithms which can quickly update the solution with the new design matrix. Our main result is a dynamic tree data structure where any update to a single matrix can be propagated quickly throughout the tree. We show that our data structure can be used to solve dynamic versions of not only Tensor Product Regression, but also Tensor Product Spline regression (which is a generalization of ridge regression) and for maintaining Low Rank Approximations for the tensor product.

☆ A Mesh for Every Moment
Roy Or-El, Jeong Joon Park, Ira Kemelmacher-Shlizerman
We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io
