☆ Quantitative Convergence of Hit-and-Run Beyond Log-Concavity via Variational Hypocoercivity
Francis Lörler, Stefan Oberdörster
We study the convergence to equilibrium of Hit-and-Run, a popular generalisation of the Gibbs sampler. To this end, we establish a novel connection between Hit-and-Run and the theory of variational hypocoercivity, an approach to establish convergence of continuous-time Markov processes. To bridge the gap between the discrete-time Hit-and-Run chain and hypocoercivity, we introduce Hit-and-Langevin, a continuous-time Markov process that approximates Hit-and-Run in an appropriate sense. Using the second-order lift and flow Poincaré inequality formulation of variational hypocoercivity, we show convergence of Hit-and-Langevin and deduce a lower bound on the spectral gap of Hit-and-Run. Notably, our analysis seamlessly extends beyond the extensively studied setting of log-concave target distributions, marking the first substantial departure from this setting beyond quasi-log-concave and uniform distributions. More broadly, this work demonstrates that discrete, non-local dynamics, such as Hit-and-Run, can be made amenable to powerful analytical methods, such as variational hypocoercivity.
☆ First-Order Entropic Sampling of Words with Prescribed Letter Counts in Linear Time
Olivier Bodini, Francis Durand
We sample, exactly and uniformly, a word of length n over the alphabet {0, . . . , r} in which the letter j occurs a prescribed positive number k j of times, from a source of fair random bits. Every exact sampler reads on average at least H = log 2 (___ n k0,...,kr )___ bits. We give a sampler that reads on average at most H fresh bits, whatever r and the counts, and that performs O(n) bit operations on average over every fixed alphabet, in a bit-RAM in which a memory access costs O(1) while arithmetic is charged bit by bit. Both bounds are optimal: the first one to first order, the second one up to a constant factor, since writing the output already costs $Θ$(n). The sampler writes the word as a Huffman tree of independent binary words, and samples each of them in one of two ways. Binary words with few ones are generated by random insertions; the rank of each inserted letter among its copies, which the Fisher-Yates shuffle generates for nothing, is uniform and independent of the word, and is given back to a recycling source of uniform integers, where it pays for the next insertions. Binary words with many ones are generated by MergeShuffle driven by blocks of $Θ$(log n) bits of entropy; a block is decoded by locating only its ones when the minority letter is rare, and otherwise, its number of ones being concentrated, by a precomputed table of the blocks of typical type, of size O( $\sqrt$ n log 4 n), the rare atypical blocks being decoded slowly.

We study online preemptive scheduling on a single machine with the objective of minimizing the total weighted flow time. Bansal and Chan (SODA 2009) showed that no deterministic online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive for this problem. We show that no randomized online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary either. This settles the remaining case of the long-standing question whether the problem admits an $O(1)$-competitive online algorithm. Quantitatively, every randomized online algorithm has a competitive ratio in $Ω(\min\{\log\log W,\log\log\log\min\{P,D,n\}\})$, where $n$ is the number of jobs and $W$, $P$, and $D$ are the ratios of the largest to the smallest job weight, size, and density (weight divided by size), respectively. The lower bound also holds with high probability, with the same asymptotic dependence on the instance parameters. For every $ρ\ge1$ and every randomized online algorithm, there is an instance on which the cost of the algorithm is at least $ρ$ times the optimal cost with probability at least $1-2^{-2^ρ}$. Both lower bounds hold even if the algorithm knows in advance the size and weight of every job in release order and, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, every interarrival time up to a factor of $1+\varepsilon$.

Lorraine A. K. Ayad, Grigorios Loukides, Solon P. Pissis
Edit distance is the standard measure of string similarity, but its quadratic-time complexity is prohibitive for long strings. Popular linear-time alternatives, such as the $q$-gram distance, or the average common substring measure (ACS) that is based on matching statistics (MS), consider the substrings shared by the two input strings but not where they occur in each string. Yet in many real-world applications, e.g., when comparing document versions or co-recorded time series, a shared substring is really relevant only if its occurrences are close in position. We introduce Location-Aware Matching Statistics (LAMAS). Given strings $X$ and $Y$ and a displacement tolerance $d$, LAMAS reports, for every position $i$ of $Y$, the longest substring starting at $i$ that occurs in $X$ at a position $j$ with $|j-i|\le d$, together with the displacement $(j-i)$. MS is the special case of LAMAS with unbounded $d$. Our main result is an algorithm that solves LAMAS in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time and space for strings of length at most $n$ and any $d$; this is optimal and matches the complexity of MS. The algorithm reduces LAMAS to predecessor and successor queries over a sliding window of suffix ranks and answers them in linear total time via a window decomposition and interval union-find. Experiments on 20 real datasets and synthetic data show that LAMAS substantially improves over MS and $q$-gram distance in similarity-based classification, top-$K$ retrieval, and clustering. It is competitive with edit distance and a constrained dynamic time warping variant in classification and generally outperforms a state-of-the-art method for top-$K$ retrieval under edit distance. Finally, our implementation of the main algorithm for LAMAS scales linearly in $n$ and does not slow down as $d$ grows.
☆ Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
Jiaqing Jiang, Nathan Ju
Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

☆ Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling
Raoof Zare Moayedi, Mohammad Hossein Yassaee, Javad B. Ebrahimi
We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.

☆ A Deterministic Polynomial-Query Protocol for Envy-Free Cake Cutting
Haris Aziz
We give a deterministic protocol that divides a heterogeneous cake completely and without envy among $n$ agents using $O(n^6\log n)$ Robertson--Webb queries in the worst case. Valuations may be arbitrary nonnegative, nonatomic measures, and bundles may be disconnected. The protocol makes $O(n)$ calls to certified trimming, which uses $O(n^5\log n)$ queries on $n$ pieces. In a certified trim, each agent receives the end part, or suffix, of a different piece without envy, and every shortened piece has a witness tie leading back to a whole piece. At each step, the witness values the shortened suffix exactly as much as her own. For pieces of positive interval length with strictly increasing suffix values, the retained suffix lengths are unique, although their holders may differ. Candidate assignments share a table of value and cut queries. If the coordinatewise median of their value estimates fails a matching test, the test identifies an agent whose value is underestimated, ruling out at least half the remaining assignments. A weighted median of cut marks lets one repair step remove a small envy while allocating almost all of the residue. For complete envy-free chore allocation, the query bound is $O(n^7\log n)$.

Hedyeh Beyhaghi, Tao Zixu He, Cameron Musco
We study learning-augmented algorithms for constrained online selection problems, including the secretary problem under matroid and knapsack constraints, and the edge-weighted online bipartite matching problem with random vertex arrivals. In each, items arrive in a uniformly random order, and their values are revealed only on arrival. The goal is to select a set of items with nearly maximum total value, subject to the constraints (matroid, knapsack, or matching). In the learning-augmented setting, item value predictions are given in advance. We seek algorithms that are both consistent, in that accurate predictions lead to near-optimal selection, and robust, in that they obtain strong worst-case bounds even when predictions are inaccurate. Building on work of Fujii and Yoshida (2024) on the learning-augmented secretary problem, we study a method that follows the predicted optimum until an item with a large enough prediction error is observed. At that point, it reverts to running a worst-case competitive algorithm. We make a simple but critical modification: the first item with a large prediction error is selected with a carefully chosen probability. With this modification, we prove a general result, showing that if the underlying worst-case algorithm is $α$-competitive for $α\in(0,1]$, this approach achieves competitive ratio $\max\{\fracα{2(1+α)},\frac{1-ε}{1+ε}\}$, where $ε$ is the maximum relative error of any prediction. That is, the algorithm is perfectly consistent, achieving competitive ratio $1$ as $ε\to 0$, and robust up to a constant factor relative to the worst-case baseline. For all three problems we study, $α= 1/e$, and our result is the first to achieve consistency and constant-factor robustness. We hope that our general analysis framework can be applied to other learning-augmented online decision-making problems.

Baruch Schieber, Hadas Shachnai, Tami Tamir
Scheduling on unrelated parallel machines under standard objectives, such as makespan minimization or max-min fairness, has posed fundamental theoretical challenges for decades. A prominent example is the longstanding factor 2 approximation barrier for the Min Makespan problem established by Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (1990). We investigate these fundamental challenges within the framework of algorithms with trusted advice. We consider a setting in which a trusted oracle is accessed once and reveals partial but entirely accurate structural information about an optimal solution. This framework allows us to quantify the improvements in approximation guarantees enabled by various trusted advice. We formalize a hierarchy of trusted advice oracles, ranging from a strong oracle that reveals the exact assignments of long jobs to a weaker oracle that indicates only which machines process such jobs. By exploiting this information, we obtain approximation guarantees beyond the classical worst-case barriers. In particular, we show that even the weakest oracle improves the approximation ratio for Min Makespan to $\sqrt{3}\approx 1.732$. We also obtain improved ratios of $(\sqrt{33}+1)/4\approx 1.686$ and $(5\sqrt{7})/8 \approx 1.654$ for Restricted Assignment and Graph Balancing, respectively. For the max-min fairness objective, known as the Santa Claus problem, we obtain a 2-approximation using our weak oracle. Finally, we show that these problems remain NP-hard to approximate within certain constant factors even with the trusted advice oracles considered. Interestingly, for the Santa Claus problem, we show a lower bound of 2 which is tight and matches the classical oracle-free bound.

The randomized greedy maximal independent set (RGMIS) algorithm processes vertices in a uniformly random order and greedily constructs an MIS. We prove that, on every $n$-vertex graph, this recursive algorithm has $O(\log n)$ query depth with high probability, even without memoization. The proof combines a bound on the total expected number of query paths with an exposure argument: paths with many two-edge shortcuts are unlikely, while the remaining paths admit sufficiently many applications of a two-hop probability bound.

The tentative allocations capture substantial welfare while controlling contention for items, and the score generator relates itemwise competition in the tentative allocations to the value of retained bundles. For example, in content moderation for social media platforms, the cost of delaying the review of a content piece is proportional to its view trajectory, which fluctuates and is a priori unknown. This bound shows that OaRC achieves asymptotic optimality for overloaded systems when the system size $N$ scales to infinity. Moreover, the bound is independent of the state-space size, which is a desirable property when job states contain contextual information. We corroborate our results with an extensive simulation study based on two holding cost patterns (online ads and user-generated content) that arise in content moderation for social media platforms. Our simulations based on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that OaRC consistently outperforms existing practice, which is based on the two canonical algorithmic principles.

Chong-Yuan Xu, Ze-Chuan Liu, Yong Xu
Simulating fermionic systems on qubit-based quantum computers often demands significant computational resources due to the requirement to map fermions to qubits. Thus, designing a fault-tolerant quantum computer that operates directly with fermions offers an effective solution to this challenge. Here, we introduce a protocol for fault-tolerant fermionic quantum computation utilizing fermion-to-fermion low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Our architecture employs a fermionic LDPC memory, which transfers its state to fermionic color code processors, where logical operations are subsequently performed. We use odd-weight logical Majorana operators to encode fermionic information in the LDPC memory and provide an algorithm for identifying these operators. Explicit code examples exhibit logical failure rates substantially below the physical error rate. We further develop two fermionic lattice surgery protocols to enable state transfer between the memory and processors. Finally, we demonstrate effective error suppression in a simulation of fermionic dynamics using the proposed protocol.

We study optimal transport between probability measures supported on the same finite metric space, where the ground cost is a distance induced by a weighted connected graph. Building on recent work showing that the resulting Kantorovich distance can be expressed as a minimization problem over the set of spanning trees of this underlying graph, we investigate the implications of this reformulation on the construction of an optimal transport plan and a dual potential based on the solution of such an optimization problem. In this setting, we derive an explicit formula for the Kantorovich potential in terms of the imbalanced cumulative mass (a generalization of the cumulative distribution in R) along an optimal spanning tree solving such a minimization problem, under a weak non-degeneracy condition on the pair of measures that guarantees the uniqueness of a dual potential. Our second contribution establishes the existence of an optimal transport plan that can be computed efficiently by a dynamic programming procedure once an optimal spanning tree is known. Finally, we propose a stochastic algorithm based on simulated annealing on the space of spanning trees to compute such an optimal spanning tree. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate the practical relevance of the proposed approach for optimal transport on finite metric spaces.

We revisit Gabow's $O(\sqrt{n} m)$ maximum cardinality matching algorithm (The Weighted Matching Approach to Maximum Cardinality Matching, Fundamenta Informaticae, 2017). It adapts the weighted matching algorithm of Gabow and Tarjan~\cite{GT91} to maximum cardinality matching. Gabow's algorithm works iteratively. In each iteration, it constructs a maximal number of edge-disjoint shortest augmenting paths with respect to the current matching and augments them. It is well-known that $O(\sqrt{n})$ iterations suffice. Each iteration consists of three parts. In the first part, the length of the shortest augmenting path is computed. In the second part, an auxiliary graph $H$ is constructed with the property that shortest augmenting paths in $G$ correspond to augmenting paths in $H$. In the third part, a maximal set of edge-disjoint augmenting paths in $H$ is determined, and the paths are lifted to and augmented to $G$. We give a new algorithm for the first part. Gabow's algorithm for the first part is derived from Edmonds' primal-dual algorithm for weighted matching. We believe that our approach is more direct and will be easier to teach. We have implemented the algorithm; the implementation is available at the companion webpage (https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/CompanionPageGenMatchingImplementation.html).
♻ ☆ Well-Conditioned Oblivious Perturbations in Linear Space
Shabarish Chenakkod, Michał Dereziński, Xiaoyu Dong, Mark Rudelson
Perturbing a deterministic $n$-dimensional matrix with small Gaussian noise is a cornerstone of smoothed analysis of algorithms [Spielman and Teng, JACM 2004], as it reduces the condition number of the input to $O(n)$, and with it the complexity of many matrix algorithms. However, when deployed algorithmically, these perturbations are expensive due to the cost of generating and storing $n^2$ Gaussian random variables. We propose a perturbation that requires generating and storing $O(n)$ random numbers in $O(\log n)$ bits of precision, and reduces the condition number of any deterministic matrix to $O(n)$, matching Gaussian perturbations. Our result takes a step towards derandomizing matrix perturbations in numerical linear algebra, and in particular, implies that we can solve an $n\times n$ linear system to within $\varepsilon$ backward error in $O(n^2\log(n)/\varepsilon)$ time using only $O(n\log n)$ random bits. In our construction, we introduce the concept of a pattern matrix, which is a dense deterministic matrix that maps all sparse vectors into dense vectors in a way that goes beyond the classical uncertainty principle of the Fourier transform. We combine this with a sparse perturbation whose entries are dependent and located in a non-uniform fashion. In order to analyze this construction, we develop new techniques for lower bounding the smallest singular value of a random matrix with dependent entries.
comment: SODA 2027
♻ ☆ Efficient space reduction techniques by optimized majority rules for the Kemeny aggregation problem
Xuan Kien Phung, Sylvie Hamel
The Kemeny aggregation problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy various fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall tau distance, which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. The NP-hard Kemeny aggregation problem admits important applications in various domains such as operations research, computational social choice, machine learning, and biology but faces a severe bottleneck in practice. In 2020, Milosz and the second author presented an approach to reduce the search space of the problem by solving the relative order of pairs of elements in those consensus rankings. In this article, we prove an optimized and fully parallelizable extension of this approach. We achieve significantly more space reduction while the parallel design reduces the time complexity from ${O}(n^3)$ to essentially ${O}(n^2)$ with significant computational speedups in practice. We then show how the constraints built by our approach can be rigorously combined with other methods such as Integer Programming and Finest Condorcet Partitioning to achieve a highly efficient, robust, and scalable solution approach to the Kemeny aggregation problem. Our methods are applicable to the more general constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem with immutable input pairwise constraints. Experiments with benchmark against the commercial solver Gurobi are performed on real and synthetic data.
♻ ☆ Strong Testability of Full Quartet Consistency with Polynomial Query Bounds
Chuang-Chieh Lin
We study dense property testing of full quartet systems on~$n$ taxa, where one resolved topology is specified for every four-set. We give an explicit polynomial-time adaptive one-sided tester using $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(2/\varepsilon)\log(1/δ))$ quartet queries to distinguish tree-like inputs from inputs that are $\varepsilon$-far from every tree-induced system, with soundness error at most $δ$, for $0<δ\leq1/3$. The bound is independent of $n$. The tester reconstructs trees on a small random sample and its verification taxa, then checks their individual attachment edges. Soundness follows by comparing with a global tree fixed by the initial sample and bounding attachment collisions through a conditional symmetry argument. Querying the complete sampled subsystem in advance also gives an explicit non-adaptive $O(\varepsilon^{-4}\log(1/δ))$ bound. A distance-preserving encoding into directed colored structures provides an additional qualitative proof through hereditary testing. For ordinary testing, we prove an $Ω(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/δ))$ query lower bound for $0<\varepsilon,δ\leq1/4$ and sufficiently large $n$. We also analyze the stronger requirement of reconstructing the exact tree on tree-like inputs, obtaining tight bounds up to constants of $Θ(n\log n+\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/δ))$ adaptively and $Θ(n^3+\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/δ))$ non-adaptively.
comment: Submitted to a journal for publication
♻ ☆ A (2 sqrt(3) - 3)-Approximation for Online and Offline Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization
Vaneet Aggarwal, Donglei Du
We obtain the approximation coefficient $α_0=2\sqrt3-3$ for maximizing nonnegative,non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed subsets of the unit cube, with queries allowed throughout the cube. This improves the previous best coefficient, $4/9$. A coordinatewise map, exponential on small coordinates and linear-fractional on large ones, turns a feasible point, the learner's state, into a feasible action whose value is at least $α_0$ times that of any feasible point, up to a linear term. No map of the state that is feasible for every down-closed set admits a larger coefficient in such a comparison. The proof combines lemmas proved by hand with finitely many sign conditions on explicit piecewise polynomials, verified in exact arithmetic. The linear term has an unbiased estimator from one noisy-gradient query, which reduces online maximization to online linear optimization. With gradient responses of bounded conditional second moment, projected ascent has expected approximate regret $O(\sqrt T)$, and online Frank--Wolfe with one linear-maximization call per round has $O(T^{3/4})$ when the responses are almost surely bounded. One noisy value per round, with bounded gradients and second-moment or almost-sure bounds on the value responses, gives $O(T^{3/4})$ and $O(T^{7/8})$, respectively. Online-to-batch conversion turns these bounds into offline guarantees. With exact values and gradients, contracting the objective toward a feasible interior point yields an expected $(α_0-\varepsilon)$-approximation for every nonnegative $C^1$ DR-submodular objective, with oracle counts polynomial in $n$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and no gradient or smoothness parameter. Sampling and standard rounding give $(α_0-\varepsilon)$-approximations for nonnegative submodular set functions under one matroid or a fixed number of knapsack constraints.
♻ ☆ One partition function call to rule them all: Efficiently computing the equilibrium landscape of multiple nucleic acid strands
Ahmed Shalaby, Damien Woods
In the nearest neighbour model of DNA/RNA binding, the partition function (PF) is a sum of Boltzmann-weighted free energies of the exponentially large set of secondary structures. Dirks et al. [SIAM review, 2007] gave a polynomial time PF algorithm for $O(1)$ strands, generalising McCaskill [Biopolymers, 1990] single-stranded case. Despite the intuition that PF may somehow encode the entire state space, thus far different approaches were required to solve various energy-landscape prediction problems. For example: finding the minimum free energy (MFE), structure(s) for $O(1)$ strands was open since 2007, and we recently solved [ICALP, 2025] via new techniques. We asked if there is a magnifiable PF algorithm [DNA31, 2025], which we answer here in the affirmative. We give an $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space algorithm, for $c=O(1)$ strands of $N$ bases, the same overhead as Dirks et al. (non-magnifiable) algorithm. However, we show that magnification allows for efficient decoding of the entire landscape, concretely: a single call to the magnifiable PF efficiently solves and improves upon a large number of problems, giving: - MFE in $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space; a considerable improvement over our $O(N^4(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^4)$ space result [ICALP 2025]. - The first polynomial time algorithm for the multi-stranded density of states problem, in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space. - The first polynomial time algorithm outputting the entire list of energy levels occupied by at least one structure (in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space), and the first algorithms for various energy landscape and counting problems. Our approach unifies the field of energy landscape prediction showing that a single, general, algorithmic framework neatly unifies a large collection of problems that practitioners care about, and required distinct techniques with worse time bounds.
♻ ☆ Faster Deterministic All-Pairs Shortest Paths with Real Edge Weights
Isaac Barouch Essayag, Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy
We give a deterministic algorithm for exact all-pairs shortest paths (APSP), that is, all distances, in directed $n$-vertex graphs with arbitrary finite real edge weights and no negative cycles. Its worst-case running time is $O(n^{2.9929729})$ with the recent rectangular matrix multiplication bound $ω(1,\tfrac12,1)=2$, and $O(n^{2.99306273})$ with earlier rectangular bounds alone; both improve the deterministic bound $O(n^{2.9997})$ and the Las Vegas expected-time bound $O(n^{2.993805})$. The algorithm runs on a real RAM whose only real-number operations are exact addition, subtraction, and comparison, each at unit cost.
comment: 50 pages. Expanded algorithm descriptions and proofs. Clarified the running-time bounds and computation model
♻ ☆ Breadth-First Search in Succinct Planar Graphs
Johannes Meintrup
An encoding for a graph class $\mathcal{G}$ is called succinct if it uses $Z_{\mathcal{G}}(n)+o(Z_{\mathcal{G}}(n))$ bits, where $Z_{\mathcal{G}}(n)$ is the information-theoretic minimum number of bits needed to distinguish between $n$-vertex graphs of $\mathcal{G}$; it is called compact if it uses $O(Z_{\mathcal{G}}(n))$ bits. For planar graphs, $Z_{\mathcal{G}}(n)=Θ(n)$. We present a succinct encoding of planar graphs that supports executing a breadth-first search directly on the encoding. The succinct encoding can be constructed in expected $O(n)$ time using $O(n)$ bits during construction; a compact variant can be constructed in deterministic $O(n)$ time using $O(n)$ bits. Once the encoding is constructed, a BFS from any start vertex can be computed in $O(n)$ time using $o(n)$ additional bits, including the space needed to represent the BFS tree. The resulting BFS tree $T$ remains available for standard tree operations, such as traversal, parent and child queries, layer queries, and lowest common ancestor queries, in constant time per query and amortized constant time per output element. The encoding also supports standard graph queries. Finally, all BFS and tree-query results generalize to separable graph classes, with graph-class-specific construction time and space for the encoding.
♻ ☆ Sublinear Time Quantum Algorithm for Attention Approximation ICLR 2026
Zhao Song, Jianfei Xue, Jiahao Zhang, Lichen Zhang
Given the query, key and value matrices $Q, K, V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, the attention module is defined as $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)=D^{-1}AV$ where $A=\exp(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})$ with $\exp(\cdot)$ applied entrywise, $D=\mathrm{diag}(A\mathbf{1}_n)$. The attention module is the backbone of modern transformers and large language models, but explicitly forming the softmax matrix $D^{-1}A$ incurs $Ω(n^2)$ time, motivating numerous approximation schemes that reduce runtime to $\widetilde O(nd)$ via sparsity or low-rank factorization. We propose a quantum data structure that approximates any row of $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)$ using only row queries to $Q, K, V$. Our algorithm preprocesses these matrices in $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-1} n^{0.5} (s_λ^{3} + s_λ^{2} d + d) + ε^{-2} s_λd)$ time, where $ε$ is the target accuracy and $s_λ$ is the $λ$-statistical dimension of the exponential kernel defined by $Q$ and $K$. Each row query can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(s_λ^2 + s_λd)$ time. If every row sum of $A$ exceeds $ε\|A\|+λ\sqrt n$, then with probability $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ the answers have Frobenius-norm error $O(β\|D^{-1}\|(ε\|A\|_F+λ\sqrt n)\|V\|_F)$. Here $β=(1-(ε\|A\|+λ\sqrt n)\|D^{-1}\|)^{-1}\geq 1$ is close to $1$ when every row sum is much larger than $ε\|A\|+λ\sqrt n$. To our knowledge, this is the first quantum data structure that approximates rows of the attention matrix in sublinear time with respect to $n$. Our approach relies on a quantum Nyström approximation of the exponential kernel, quantum multivariate mean estimation for computing $D$, and quantum sampling of the rows of $V$ by their squared norms, with a median over independent samples, for the multiplication with $V$.
comment: ICLR 2026. This version corrects the main theorem: the preprocessing time, the row-query count, and the error bound, whose $λ\sqrt{n}$ term is additive and which needs large row sums and a full-rank Nystrom factor. The product with V now samples rows by squared norms, as the published leverage-score step and its boosting were invalid, and the error proof is completed
♻ ☆ Graph-based Nearest Neighbors with Dynamic Updates via Random Walks ICLR 2026
Nina Mishra, Yonatan Naamad, Tal Wagner, Lichen Zhang
Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANN) is a common way to retrieve relevant search results, especially now in the context of large language models and retrieval augmented generation. One of the most widely used algorithms for ANN is based on constructing a multi-layer graph over the dataset, called the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). While this algorithm supports insertion of new data, it does not support deletion of existing data. Moreover, deletion algorithms described by prior work come at the cost of increased query latency, decreased recall, or prolonged deletion time. In this paper, we propose a new theoretical framework for graph-based ANN based on random walks. We then utilize this framework to analyze a randomized deletion approach that approximately preserves hitting time statistics compared to the graph before deleting the point. However, this guarantee needs at least as many edge samples as there are edges in the clique over the neighbors of the deleted point. We then turn this theoretical framework into a deterministic deletion algorithm, and show that it provides a better tradeoff between query latency, recall, deletion time, and memory usage through an extensive collection of experiments.
comment: ICLR 2026. This version withdraws the claim that linearly many patch edges suffice: the hitting-time guarantee for randomized deletion needs at least as many edge samples as there are edges in the clique over the neighbors of the deleted point. It also adds a missing hypothesis to the hitting-time theorem and corrects the star-mesh step and the edge sparsification lemma
♻ ☆ A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
Ali Lotfi, Ian McQuillan, Steven Rayan
L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.
comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Published in Research in the Mathematical Sciences (2026)
♻ ☆ Tolerant Testing for Bipartiteness and Unique Games
Yuichi Yoshida
We give a tolerant bipartiteness tester in the adjacency-list model on arbitrary simple undirected graphs. Let \(n\) be the number of vertices and \(m>0\) the known number of edges. For \(0<\varepsilon<ρ<1/10\), write \(λ_ρ:=ρ/(1+\log(1/ρ))\). If \(\varepsilon\log n\le cλ_ρ^2\) for a sufficiently small absolute constant \(c>0\), the tester distinguishes graphs that can be made bipartite by deleting at most an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of their edges from graphs requiring deletion of at least a \(ρ\) fraction, using \[ \widetilde O\!\left( \frac{\sqrt{n/ρ}}{λ_ρ^{3/2}} +\frac1{λ_ρ^2} +\frac{n}{\sqrt m\,λ_ρ}\right) \] queries, where the suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in \(n,1/ρ\). For fixed \(ρ\), the query bound is \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n+n/\sqrt m)\). We prove an \(Ω(\sqrt n+n/\sqrt m)\) query lower bound. The tester extends to Unique Games over any alphabet size \(Q\ge2\), under the same tolerance condition with \(c\) independent of \(Q\), with a polylogarithmic overhead in \(Q\) in the query complexity. Each constrained neighbor query returns the entire edge permutation.
♻ ☆ Catalan Hashing: Efficient Linear Probing for Variable-Length Items
Alex Conway, Hanna Komlós, William Kuszmaul
A defining feature of the linear-probing hash table is its spatial locality: at load factor $1 - \varepsilon$, the hash table can be implemented so that each operation scans a single contiguous region of expected size $O(1/\varepsilon)$ (this is known as the \emph{scan cost}). This guarantee, however, relies on all items having unit size. In this paper, we ask whether it is possible to achieve a similar guarantee, but in a hash table that stores items of arbitrary lengths $|x| \ge 1$. The main result of the paper is a new hash table called \emph{Catalan hashing}, which supports amortized expected scan cost $O(|x|/\varepsilon)$ for positive queries, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ for negative queries, and $O(|x|\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{1+δ}|x|)$ for insertions/deletions, for any constant $δ> 0$. As a corollary, we obtain the same bounds in the cache-oblivious model, with a scan cost of $S$ translating to $1 + O(S/B)$ I/Os. Along the way, we introduce several high-level techniques that may be of independent interest; this includes a novel way of using erasure codes in order to perform write optimization within a hash table, and a connection to scheduling that allows us to place elements in a way which avoids clustering at high load factors.
comment: minor updates
♻ ☆ Faster CONGEST Approximation Algorithms for Maximum Weighted Independent Set in Sparse Graphs
Salwa Faour, Fabian Kuhn
We give deterministic distributed CONGEST algorithms for the weighted version of the problem in trees and graphs of bounded arboricity. All weights are nonnegative integers bounded by $n^{O(1)}$. For trees and $\log(n)/n<\varepsilon\leq1/8$, we prove that the task of deterministically computing a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate solution to the maximum weight independent set (MWIS) problem has a tight $Θ(\log^*(n)/\varepsilon)$ complexity. The lower bound already holds on unweighted oriented paths. The upper bound holds even for unrooted trees. For graphs $G=(V,E)$ of arboricity $β>1$, we give two algorithms. If the sum of all node weights is $w(V)$, we show that for any $0<\varepsilon\leq1/2$, an independent set of weight at least $(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\frac{w(V)}{4β}$ can be computed in $O(\log^2(β/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon + \log(β/\varepsilon)\cdot\log^* n)$ rounds. We further show that for any $0<\varepsilon\leq1/2$, an independent set of weight at least $(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\frac{w(V)}{2β+1}$ can be computed in $O(\log^3(β)\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2\cdot\log n)$ rounds. For $\varepsilon=ω(1/\sqrtβ)$, this significantly improves on a recent result of Gil [OPODIS '23], whose algorithm yields a $1/\lfloor(2+\varepsilon)β\rfloor$-approximation in $O(β/\varepsilon\cdot\log n)$ rounds when its accuracy dependence is tracked. As an intermediate step to our result, we design an algorithm to compute an independent set of total weight at least $(1-\varepsilon)\cdot\sum_{v\in V}\frac{w(v)}{°(v)+1}$ in time $O(\log^3(Δ)\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon + \log^* n)$, where $Δ$ is the maximum degree of the graph and logarithmic runtime factors are lower-bounded by one.
comment: 30 pages. Revised full version of the OPODIS 2026 paper
♻ ☆ Greedy BPE with Replacement Counts Achieves the Tight Approximation Ratio $(1-e^{-2})/2$
Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds the tokenisers of many language models by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. Kozma and Voderholzer showed that $k$ greedy merges save, in the worst case, between $1/3$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.43233$ of what the best $k$ merges save, and asked for the exact constant. We resolve this question for the replacement-count rule they analyse. For every string and weighted word table, every budget $k$, and every tie-breaking rule, greedy saves at least $\frac12(1-(1-2/k)^k)$ of the optimum. This establishes the exact worst-case approximation ratio $(1-e^{-2})/2$, approached as $k\to\infty$ but never attained. The proof is based on a shadow inequality: after $i$ greedy steps, the optimum is at most $2G_i+kg_{i+1}$, where $G_i$ is greedy's saving so far and $g_{i+1}$ its next gain. We also show that the worst-case ratio at budget $k$ exceeds the limiting constant by $Θ(k^{-1/2})$. For the overlapping-count rule used by deployed trainers, we prove a lower bound greater than $0.38954$ and an asymptotic upper bound of approximately $0.40407$; determining its exact constant remains open.
comment: 58 pages. v3 supersedes v2 (0.391 bound), establishing the exact worst-case approximation ratio for replacement-count BPE, a finite-budget convergence result, and bounds for overlapping-count BPE. Code and certificates: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24451469
♻ ☆ GreedTok Is a 0.3287-Approximation, and Greedy Tokenizers Lose Order $1/\log k$ on Fixed Alphabets
Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju
A tokenizer's vocabulary is built once and used on every input, so it matters how much compression a greedy construction can lose. We study two greedy constructions: GreedTok (Lim et al., 2025), which adds the string that saves the most tokens, and byte-pair encoding (BPE), which merges a most frequent adjacent pair. We prove that GreedTok saves at least $0.3287$ of the optimal number of tokens saved on every corpus, while no constant above $0.33862$ is possible. The key idea is that, given the order of greedy's choices, the damage inside an optimal token is fixed by two numbers. On a fixed alphabet both algorithms are asymptotically optimal and their worst deficit with budget $k$ has order $1/\log k$: one counting argument gives the upper bound for both, and one binary corpus, whose first greedy commitment erases a boundary between optimal tokens, gives the matching lower bound for both (for GreedTok, on its committed segmentation), even if greedy's continuation may use almost twice the budget. For BPE on one binary string, a forced first merge can cost $Ω(k)$ final tokens, yet $2k+3$ rules always repair it.
comment: 69 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. v2 adds fixed-alphabet results for GreedTok and greedy BPE (deficit of order 1/log k, tight), a binary-string repair theorem for BPE, and an EPTAS for fixed alphabets; the 0.3287 bound is unchanged. Code and checkers: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24451478

☆ HoloSplat: Real-Time Token Streaming for Feed-Forward Human Reconstruction
Chaofan Li, Qihan Ding, Shihan Wang, Zhehao Shen, Boyu Shen, Quanyu Chen, Haoyu Wu, Lan Xu, Xin Lou
Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.
comment: 43 pages including supplementary material, 20 figures. Project page: https://heaticy.github.io/HoloSplat/
☆ CrownFusion: 3D Dental Crown Generation Using Geometry Images and Latent Diffusion MICCAI 2026
Johan Ziruo Ye, Xingguang Yan, Søren Hauberg, Angel X. Chang, Hao Zhang, Peter Lempel Søndergaard
We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.
comment: Accepted at MICCAI 2026. 11 pages, 6 figures. Equal contribution: J. Z. Ye and X. Yan. Project page: https://crownfusion.github.io/
☆ DiffSimp: Differentiable Mesh Simplification for Gradient-Based Low-Poly Modeling
Seonghun Oh
Differentiable mesh extraction enables gradient-based optimization of detailed 3D geometry across diverse tasks. However, compact meshes are commonly obtained through post-processing simplification, leaving simplification-induced errors outside upstream optimization. We introduce DiffSimp, a training-free, drop-in differentiable mesh simplification layer built on QEM-based parallel edge collapse, enabling existing geometry optimization pipelines to optimize their final simplified meshes. We formulate simplification under a fixed collapse history as a locally differentiable collapse map, enabling gradient propagation without relaxing discrete collapse decisions. We combine fast, high-quality parallel simplification with a factorized backward formulation that exploits differentiable vertex quadrics and quadric reduction forests for efficient gradient propagation. Experiments on low-poly mesh reconstruction and inverse rendering demonstrate improved fidelity over post-processing simplification, with additional gains from gradient propagation that increase under tighter vertex budgets. DiffSimp supports diverse geometry optimization frontends, with 1.00-1.25$\times$ the end-to-end runtime of unsimplified baselines in evaluated pipelines.
☆ Learning the Next Best Move with Visual Diffusion Models
Amir Razlighi, Ali Mahdavi Amiri, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Andrey Voynov, Daniel Cohen-Or
In this paper, we show that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move (NBM) in tasks requiring sequential reasoning and lookahead, without explicitly exploring future steps or exhaustive searching at inference. Previous work demonstrated that these models can generate complete solutions to geometric and reasoning problems. Here, we show that simple fine-tuning on visual state--NBM pairs enables a pretrained model to select actions whose value depends on consequences several steps ahead. Each move is predicted directly in image space from the current state, without an explicit symbolic representation or search procedure. Repeated NBM predictions then construct a solution one decision at a time. We demonstrate this capability on chess puzzles and tile-based pathfinding, and show that it extends to Connect Four, Go and billiards. In chess, the model predicts legal moves and finds the best move far more often than by recalling similar training positions, including piece sacrifices whose benefit emerges only through later tactical continuations. In pathfinding, it constructs shortest paths on uniform-cost maps and cost-optimal routes across terrain tiles with different traversal costs, choosing longer routes when they are cheaper overall. These costs are learned implicitly from examples, without numerical cost supervision. These results show that direct visual move prediction can support globally informed decisions and successful sequential problem solving.
comment: project page: https://amirhossein-razlighi.github.io/next_best_move
☆ Fairness-optimized interlacing knots for even-degree periodic B-spline interpolation
Shutao Tang, Zixuan Zhao
Interpolating an ordered set of points by a B-spline curve is a fundamental operation in computer-aided geometric design. Most of the literature addresses open curves, where the Schoenberg--Whitney condition characterizes a nonsingular collocation matrix and averaging is the standard way to choose the knot vector. Periodic B-spline interpolation has received much less attention, and the open-curve algorithms cannot be transferred directly. No theoretical criterion is available for choosing the knots, and the few existing constructions, such as the shifting and energy methods, remain empirical, with neither a theoretical guarantee nor a supporting analysis. This paper addresses this gap for even degrees. We prove that for every even degree $p\ge2$ the periodic collocation matrix is nonsingular whenever the domain knots and the interpolation parameters interlace, in either of two admissible orderings, for arbitrarily nonuniform parameters. Rather than singling out one knot vector, this sufficient condition delimits an $n$-parameter family of admissible knot vectors and provides the theoretical foundation for knot selection that periodic interpolation has lacked. It also explains why the empirical shifting method is solvable, previously justified only by an incorrect diagonal-dominance argument. We then exploit the remaining freedom to place the knots by fairness optimization, which preserves admissibility at every iterate and leads to the methods Opt-R and Opt-L. On four closed shapes with irregularly distributed points these methods achieve a fairness comparable to the shifting and energy methods, improve on them in several cases, and offer guarantees that no empirical construction provides.
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures
☆ Tri-DNO: Trilateral Diffusion Noise Optimization for 3D Human Object Interaction
Paul Hinzer, Niklas Gard, Anna Hilsmann, Peter Eisert
Generating realistic 3D human object interactions (HOI) is essential for applications, such as augmented or virtual reality (AR/VR) or character animation of interactive entertainment. A particular challenge lies in the faithful generation of hand grasps in human object interaction scenes, where even minor geometric inconsistencies, such as insufficient contact or interpenetration, can significantly compromise realism. While diffusion-based generative models have shown promising results in HOI synthesis, ensuring physically plausible hand-object interactions remains challenging. We present Tri-DNO, a diffusion noise optimization strategy to sample from a pretrained multimodal HOI diffusion model, improving hand-object contact. Rather than modifying or retraining the generative model, our approach iteratively optimizes the initial noise of the diffusion generator, thereby generating firm hand object contact, while mitigating penetration and keeping the hand position realistic. Experiments on the GRAB dataset demonstrate improvements over the baseline in grasp quality without additional model training or increased computational cost compared to existing methods. We further demonstrate the applicability of our approach to practical media production scenarios.

Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.

Even in a controlled environment, reconstruction is severely underconstrained: appearance is view dependent, motion is non-rigid, and the unobserved volume admits many geometries. These rotational priors allow us to reconstruct otherwise unobserved structure. We evaluate reconstruction accuracy by computing novel-view synthesis accuracy on a held out camera view: Tornado4D outperforms frame-by-frame 3DGS and video-based 4DGS by a considerable margin.

♻ ☆ Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate

Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in $R^2$ (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

♻ ☆ Constant-Memory Differentiable Light Tracing
Linas Beresna, Eugene Fiume
Reverse-mode differentiation of Monte Carlo light transport naively stores a computation graph that grows with path length, ruling it out for deep or high-sample simulation. Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) removes that cost for viewpoint path tracing by reconstructing paths from their seeds and replaying them backward in constant memory. The construction rests on a one-path-one-pixel property that light tracing lacks: one light path contributes to many pixels, and its per-vertex adjoints cannot be recovered during replay from constant-size state. We show this prevents a direct extension of PRB, and that buffering the per-vertex data stays linear in path length. We then evaluate two constant-memory formulations. Reservoir Light Replay Backpropagation compresses a path's sensor connections into one representative by weighted reservoir sampling, keeping two passes at the cost of a sampling decision. LRB-3-pass adds a traversal that accumulates downstream adjoints first, keeping every connection and matching naive automatic differentiation in expectation. Both support differentiating with fixed or parameter-dependent path sampling (detached and attached), and both extend to participating media. We validate against naive AD and finite differences, characterize the memory and runtime trade-offs, and recover specular and volumetric caustics by light tracing alone.

♻ ☆ Conformal tubular parameterization and toroidal bending of tube-like surfaces
Shunyu Yao, Gary P. T. Choi
Tube-like surfaces are widely encountered in geometry processing, engineering structures, and medical anatomy, yet their intrinsic longitudinal and circumferential information is not well preserved by conventional planar annular or rectangular parameterization domains. In this work, we propose a new conformal parameterization framework for open tube-like surfaces with two boundary components. The proposed method first constructs a fixed-boundary tubular parameterization by cutting the input mesh, computing a disk-to-parallelogram quasi-conformal map, and lifting the result to a cylindrical surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$. To reduce residual distortion introduced near the cut seam, we further introduce a localized quasi-conformal correction scheme formulated on an annular domain, which improves conformality while leaving regions away from the seam unchanged. To handle noisy or irregular input boundaries, we also develop a free-boundary variant based on boundary extension and cycle-Laplacian smoothing, allowing the prescribed boundary constraints to be imposed on artificial outer rings rather than directly on the original surface. Finally, as an optional post-processing step, we derive two conformal toroidal bending maps that embed the tubular parameterization into toroidal geometries without altering its conformal structure. Experiments on synthetic tube meshes and real vascular surfaces demonstrate that the proposed framework produces low-distortion parameterizations, effectively mitigates seam-induced artifacts, improves robustness for boundary-noisy inputs, and provides flexible tubular and toroidal target domains for downstream surface processing tasks.

The GP learns from regional graph representations and PPA feedback. Using the GP's predictions and predictive uncertainty, Bayesian optimization (BO) provides guidance that an LLM Router combines with circuit analysis to choose how to address each region's bottlenecks. Self-improving LLM workers then optimize the RTL or synthesis algorithms in their assigned regions, and their regional changes are greedily integrated into the current design configuration. Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex reasoning tasks, yet their inference efficiency is fundamentally constrained by the rapid growth of the KV cache. As reasoning contexts extend to hundreds of thousands of tokens, the key-value (KV) cache becomes the dominant contributor to both memory footprint and bandwidth demand, tightly coupling computation with memory utilization and thereby limiting scalability. Existing compression methods, such as quantization and eviction, alleviate capacity pressure but remain purely algorithmic, often introducing additional passes and compute overhead that reduce system efficiency. This paper presents Gossamer, a KV cache compression architecture for reasoning LLMs that bridges the algorithm--system--hardware gap. Gossamer introduces a unified utility-based action framework that dynamically selects compression operations, quantization, merging, or eviction, under a constant KV cache budget. Through cross-domain co-design, we fuse cosine-similarity estimation directly into the attention computation, exploiting idle compute cycles to perform similarity evaluation without latency or bandwidth cost. Under tight memory constraints, Gossamer sustains reasoning quality comparable to uncompressed inference while improving end-to-end throughput by up to 16.7$\times$ over uncompressed baselines, 5.5$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ over the quantization-based Oaken and Ecco, and 1.8$\times$ over the eviction-based R-KV.

Iterative updates of Verilog code, clock-gating inference, and analysis of clock-gating efficiency (CGE) are time-consuming and pose challenges to RTL designers. LLM-assisted automatic refinement of Verilog code for improving CGE is proposed. Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

The reason is a property that CXL requires of the fabric: a modified line is written back before another host accesses it. Whatever a surviving host has seen is then on the device, and our crash condition lets a crash drop operations that only the crashed host observed. We prove the claim for operations that take effect in a single store, and test it on small instances of models of three published designs, whose operations store several times. A lock table needs no flush to keep the locks of surviving hosts. A persistent hash index keeps every operation a survivor has observed, and in two workloads it writes fewer than half as many lines to the device as its published code does. An allocator's flush of each new reference is neither sufficient nor necessary for the survivors' safety: the allocator lacks ordering flushes, one of them when a reference changes hands.

Finally, the viability of OpenVADL for design space exploration is demonstrated in a case study on CRC32 checksum computation for the RISC-V ISA.

Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is PSPACE-complete for general token automata and decidable in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.

♻ ☆ Fuss-free cumulative universes: theory and practice
Raphaël Sterbac, Jonathan Sterling
Universes are central to dependent type theory, and they are notoriously difficult to handle in a way that is both correct and usable. We propose a new "fuss-free" generalised algebraic presentation for polymorphic cumulative universes that dispenses with the intricate theory of coherent universe coercions in favour of a simpler formulation, which we prove equivalent by means of a normalisation theorem for the former. We study the fuss-free formulation by means of (1) an abstract specification of its bidirectional elaboration algorithm, and (2) a concrete implementation in Haskell. We also describe and implement an extension of the fuss-free universe hierarchy with a judgemental notion of datatype description from which prior notions of cumulative inductive type may be derived.
comment: Extended version of a paper to appear in POPL 2027
♻ ☆ Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation (Extended Version)
Michael Schwarz, Zhendong Ang, Umang Mathur
Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.
comment: Accepted to POPL '27; Extended version with appendices
♻ ☆ Constrained Code Generation with Diffusion Language Models
Lize Shao, Michael Cardei, Zichen Xie, Ferdinando Fioretto, Wenxi Wang
Diffusion language models (DLMs) are a powerful, emerging paradigm for code generation. They construct programs through iterative refinement of partially corrupted token sequences and enable parallel token refinement. Importantly, this paradigm exposes a global program state at each denoising step, which provides a natural intervention point for enforcing program-level functionality and security constraints, guiding the generation before the final code is committed. Building on this observation, the paper introduces Constrained Diffusion for Code (CDC), an inference-time neurosymbolic framework that integrates constraint satisfaction directly into the reverse denoising process without retraining the base diffusion model. CDC augments the base diffusion sampler with constraint-aware denoising operators that combine mathematical optimization with program analysis to identify constraint-relevant regions of the intermediate program state and locally adjust the denoising trajectory, steering generation toward feasible programs while remaining close to the base model. Across code generation benchmarks, CDC consistently improves constraint satisfaction in functional correctness, security, and even syntax, outperforming diffusion and autoregressive baselines with less corrective computation and more localized edits.
Data Structures and Algorithms 19
☆ Improved Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Path TSP and Ordered TSP
Morteza Alimi, Michael Ruderer
In Multi-Path TSP, given a metric and $k$ pairs of vertices $(s_i,t_i)$, where $k$ is part of the input, we seek $s_i$--$t_i$ paths of minimum total length that together visit all vertices. Ratios below $2$ were known only for graphic metrics and special cases such as multiple depots ($s_i=t_i$); in general metrics, the best ratio was $1+2e^{-1/2}\approx2.213$, by a randomized algorithm of Böhm, Friggstad, Mömke and Spoerhase [SODA 2025]. We give a deterministic algorithm with ratio $\frac{5e-2}{3e-2}<1.8833$ relative to a restriction of their LP relaxation, bounding its integrality gap by the same constant. For Ordered TSP, where a tour must visit $k$ given vertices in a prescribed cyclic order, we compute tours within $1+\frac{e}{2(e-1)}<1.7910$ times the value of the LP relaxation of Armbruster, Mnich and Nägele [APPROX 2024], improving $\frac32+\frac1e\approx1.868$ on both the ratio and the integrality gap. Our algorithms sample a tree for every pair (for Ordered TSP, every two consecutive given vertices) from an LP solution, but keep only the path between the two endpoints. Our main lemma shows that, for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights, a cheapest forest connecting all vertices to these paths has expected weight at most $1/e$ times that of a cheapest forest rooted at the endpoints plus $(1-1/e)$ times the expected weight of the discarded branches. For Multi-Path TSP, we use the weights of a primal--dual growth process that Zhao, Liu and Xiao [arXiv 2026] designed for multiple depots; in these weights, the connecting forest also pays for part of correcting its degree parities.
☆ Two Rounds Are Already Hard for Loop-Free Updates of Routing Trees
Klaus-Tycho Foerster
Updating a routing tree can create loops even when the old and new trees lead to the same destination. A controller chooses which routers update in each round, but their updates may finish in any order. Strong loop freedom therefore requires every partial completion to be acyclic. We show that deciding whether two rounds suffice is NP-complete, even when a safe three-round schedule is supplied. The proof is a linear-size reduction from 3-SAT with one old clause spine and four routers per variable. Three types of mixed cycles enforce consistent literal choices and clause satisfaction. For every nonempty input formula, the constructed instance needs exactly two rounds if the formula is satisfiable and exactly three otherwise.
☆ An $n^{1/O(\log^* n)}$ Lower Bound for Online Coloring of $k$-Colorable Graphs
Sajad Faghfoor Maghrebi
In online coloring, the vertices of a graph arrive one at a time with their edges to earlier vertices, and each vertex must be colored irrevocably on arrival. For graphs promised to be $k$-colorable, with $k\ge 3$ fixed, the best deterministic algorithms use $n^{1-Θ(1/k^2)}$ colors, while the best lower bound was Vishwanathan's $Ω(\log^{k-1}n)$ from 1990 until Li recently proved $2^{Ω((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})}$. For every fixed $k\ge 3$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we prove a lower bound of $n^{1/(\log^*n+3)}$ colors for deterministic online algorithms on $n$-vertex $k$-colorable graphs, and the same lower bound in expectation for randomized online algorithms. Both bounds hold on a single triangle-free $3$-colorable graph: even an algorithm that is shown this graph in advance, but is not told which of its vertices each arriving vertex is, can be forced to use this many colors by a suitable arrival order. The hard instances are iterated blow-ups of a clique, in which every vertex becomes a block of independent vertices and every edge a private server in the earlier block; each blow-up keeps the forced colors and replaces the chromatic number $χ$ by about $\logχ$, so about $\log^*n$ blow-ups bring it down to $k$. We also show that deterministic lower bounds for different values of $k\ge 3$ are polynomially equivalent, and that no adversary presenting such iterated blow-ups can force more than $n^{1/(\log^*n-O(1))}$ colors. All numbered results are formalized in Lean 4.

☆ Faster Directed SSSP on Digraphs with Random Sparse Supports or Few DFS Exceptions
Valery, Grishin, Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy
We study exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) in directed graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs and nonnegative real weights, in the comparison-addition model. This paper continues our earlier work, which gave a deterministic algorithm that takes $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4})$ time when $m=O(n)$ and $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{5/8})$ time when $m=Θ(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$. Our two deterministic algorithms compute the distances on every input and take $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time on two families of inputs, one per density. The support of an input is its underlying simple undirected graph. When $m=O(n)$, the first algorithm takes $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time if no two simple cycles of the support with fewer than $P$ vertices share a vertex, where $P=Θ(\sqrt{\log n})$ depends only on the support. For fixed $c>0$, a uniformly random graph with $n$ vertices and $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ edges has this property with probability at least $1-n^{-1+o(1)}$, and the bound then holds for every choice of one or both directions of each edge, all weights and every source. The second family is defined through the depth-first search tree of the support that starts at the source and visits neighbours in identifier order. For fixed $k\ge1$, call a set $Y$ of exceptional vertices $k$-feasible if, for each nonroot vertex, at most $k$ of its proper ancestors are joined to its subtree by arcs whose endpoints avoid $Y$ and whose underlying edges lie outside the DFS tree. Given $k$ but not such a set, the second algorithm takes, for every $k$-feasible set $Y$ of total out-degree $d^+(Y)$, time $O_k(n+m+(1+|Y|)\log n+\sqrt{(n+m)d^+(Y)\log n})$. When $m=Θ(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$, this is $O_k(n\sqrt{\log n})$ if some $k$-feasible set has $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ vertices and total out-degree $O(n/\sqrt{\log\log n})$.

☆ Asymptotically Optimal Representation of Tree-Like Graphs
Johannes Fischer
We show how to represent a graph with $n$ nodes, $m=n+k=O(n)$ edges, and $h\le k$ nodes with more than one incoming edge in asymptotically optimal space, in a way that supports basic navigational operations quickly.
☆ Randomized MST Certification beyond Cacti
Sina Ghasemi Nezhad
We study minimum spanning tree certification under explorable edge uncertainty. Edge weights lie in open intervals or singleton sets, and querying an edge reveals its weight at a known positive cost. On general graphs the best known randomized competitive ratio is $1+1/\sqrt2$, while the optimal ratio $3/2$ is known only for cacti. We go beyond cacti in two ways, with conditions that refer to the uncertain edges outside the upper-limit tree rather than to the graph alone. For unit query costs we give a $3/2$-competitive algorithm, which is best possible, whenever every block has at most two such edges; this includes all graphs whose blocks are cycles or theta graphs. The algorithm replaces the constant budget of the water-filling method by budgets chosen with lookahead to the next fundamental cycle. For arbitrary positive query costs and every fixed $k\ge1$, we obtain ratio $1+\sqrt{k/(2(k+1))}$ whenever every block has at most $k$ such edges, in particular when every block has cycle rank at most $k$. This is below $1+1/\sqrt2$ for every $k$, and we show that it is the best ratio attainable with a constant water-filling budget.
☆ Exponential memory/query-complexity tradeoffs in high-accuracy feasibility problems
Jialin Yu, Moïse Blanchard
We prove memory/query-complexity tradeoff lower bounds for the feasibility problem, where the goal is to find a point within an $ε$-ball hidden in the unit $d$-dimensional ball, with access to a separation oracle. This problem admits three regimes: the low-accuracy regime $ε\geq 1/\sqrt d$ where memory does not play a role, the medium-accuracy regime $1/\sqrt d\geq ε\geq e^{-Ω(d\ln d)}$ where prior works identified strong memory/query-complexity separations, and the high-accuracy regime $ε\leq e^{-Ω(d\ln d)}$ for which much less is known. In this regime, low-memory algorithms with significantly faster convergence rates than gradient descent have been developed in [BZJ24]: for accuracy $ε$ and any $δ\in[0,1]$, these require $d^{1+δ}\ln \frac1ε$ memory bits and use $\left(d\ln\frac1ε\right)^{O(d^{1-δ})}$ oracle queries. In comparison, gradient descent uses the same memory for $δ=0$ but requires $1/ε^2$ oracle queries. On the lower-bound side, no non-trivial memory/query-complexity tradeoff was known: the best lower bound remained the historical memory-independent bound $Ω(d\ln \frac1ε)$ from [NYD83]. We make progress towards characterizing the memory landscape in this high-accuracy regime by showing that for any $δ\in[0,1]$, any algorithm with $d^{1+δ}\ln\frac1ε$ bits of memory uses at least $\left(d\ln\frac1ε\right)^{\widetildeΩ(d^{(1-δ)/8})}$ oracle calls. This result justifies the seemingly peculiar exponential-in-$d$ dependence of oracle complexity for the aforementioned low-memory algorithms. In particular, our result shows that for high-accuracy feasibility problems, insufficient memory does result in an exponential price in the dimension for the query-complexity.
