☆ A Local-to-Global Approximation Framework for Covering Disjointness-Compliable Set Families
Jingyang Zhao, Mingyu Xiao
Many network design problems can be formulated as covering a family of vertex sets by edges. We develop a local-to-global approximation framework for disjointness-compliable families with polynomial-time membership tests. A class of vertices is deficient if it belongs to the family and feasible otherwise. Our local problem seeks a minimum-cost tree that connects one deficient class to feasible classes so that their union is feasible. If this local problem admits a polynomial-time $α$-approximation, then the covering problem admits a polynomial-time $(1+\varepsilon)(\sqrt{2}+\sqrtα)^2$-approximation for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Our algorithm first connects deficient vertices that are difficult to separate and then handles regions containing one deficient class at a time. To bound the total local cost, we compare the local trees with a feasible forest. We delete edges of this forest after using them in the bound, so each is counted at most once even when regions overlap. As applications, we obtain polynomial-time $(8+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for generalized point-to-point connection and multiroot quota tree, including multiroot $k$-minimum spanning tree. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-time constant-factor approximations for both problems. We also obtain a randomized approximation for multiroot covering Steiner that has the same asymptotic ratio as the known approximation for its single-root version.
☆ On the Complexity of Orientable Domination
Hans L. Bodlaender, Tatsuya Gima, Yasuaki Kobayashi, Futaba Mizuno, Yuto Okada, Yota Otachi
The orientable domination number of an undirected graph $G$ is the maximum over all orientations $D$ of $G$ of the minimum size of a dominating set of $D$. In this paper, we look at the problem to decide if the orientable domination number of a given undirected graph $G$ is at least a given integer $\ell$. We show that this problem is complete for the class $Σ_2^P$, is fixed-parameter tractable by treewidth, and has a polynomial kernel parameterized by vertex cover number.

☆ Frequency Estimation from the Internal State of the Boyer-Moore Majority Vote Algorithm
Saeed Momeni, Mohsen Hooshmand
The Boyer-Moore Majority Vote algorithm identifies a majority candidate in a single pass over a data stream using constant memory O(1) and linear processing time O(n). While the classic algorithm identifies a candidate without directly estimating its frequency, its internal register states retain information about item occurrences during execution. This work investigates a frequency estimator derived directly from these internal counters. We establish the conditions under which the counter state enables exact recovery of the frequency of the majority element and characterize the estimation error when these conditions are not satisfied. In particular, we analyze the effect of stream ordering on the estimator and identify delayed-arrival configurations, such as Majority-Delayed sequences, that can lead to systematic estimation errors. We further derive the error behavior associated with late-arriving majority blocks and empirically evaluate the estimator across multiple stream topologies. The results demonstrate that the internal state of the Boyer-Moore algorithm can provide frequency information without increasing its O(1) space complexity. At the same time, its accuracy depends critically on the ordering of elements in the input stream.
♻ ☆ Approximating TSP walks in subcubic graphs
Michael C. Wigal, Youngho Yoo, Xingxing Yu
We prove that every simple 2-connected subcubic graph on $n$ vertices with $n_2$ vertices of degree 2 has a TSP walk of length at most $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$, confirming a conjecture of Dvořák, Král', and Mohar. This bound is best possible; there are infinitely many subcubic and cubic graphs whose minimum TSP walks have lengths $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$ and $\frac{5n}{4} - 2$ respectively. We characterize the extremal subcubic examples meeting this bound. We also give a quadratic-time combinatorial algorithm for finding such a TSP walk. In particular, we obtain a $\frac{5}{4}$-approximation algorithm for the graphic TSP on simple cubic graphs, improving on the previously best known approximation ratio of $\frac{9}{7}$.

♻ ☆ Packed-Ring Queues: Lock-Free and Wait-Free Concurrent Queues on GPU
Pratheek Prakash Shetty, Thomas R. W. Scogland, Wu-chun Feng
Concurrent queues are a foundational building block of parallel programming. On CPUs, decades of research have produced queue designs with well-understood correctness and progress guarantees -- from lock-free rings to wait-free constructions. On GPUs, where queues increasingly sit on the critical path of device-side task graphs and GPU-initiated I/O, no comparable foundation exists: SIMT execution serializes divergent retries across a warp; tens of thousands of threads contend on the same counter words; the double-width atomics that several CPU designs assume are absent; and GPU memory models are weakly ordered, so the classical algorithms do not transfer unchanged. We present the packed-ring queues (PRQs) -- two linearizable, bounded GPU queues that represent each compound atomic state in one native word of at most 64 bits: (1) PRQ-LF, a lock-free ring whose warp-batched fast path issues one atomic per warp on each of the queue's contended words, and (2) PRQ-WF, a wait-free ring in which peer threads cooperatively complete any operation that falls behind. To the best of our knowledge, PRQ-WF is the first GPU concurrent queue whose wait-freedom is proved as a theorem, with no assumption about how the GPU schedules threads. Across four GPUs from two vendors (NVIDIA A100 and GH200, AMD MI210 and MI300A), PRQ-LF outperforms the blocking Broker Queue by 5.0-20.4x at 32K threads, and PRQ-WF sustains throughput under producer/consumer imbalance where a prior design completes fewer than 0.1% of its attempts.
♻ ☆ Tight Bounds for Distance-Unbiased Sorting
Mats Bierwirth, Carola Doerr, Johannes Lengler
We study elitist randomized local search for sorting permutations. In this model, each iteration considers a possible exchange of two positions. The entries are exchanged if and only if they are in the wrong order. We introduce \emph{distance-unbiased} selection rules, which may choose an arbitrary distribution over exchange distances but sample uniformly among all pairs at each chosen distance. For static rules, we prove that the optimal worst-case high-probability runtime is $Θ(n(\log n)^2)$. This establishes the asymptotic optimality of the harmonic sorter within this class and partially resolves an open question of Olesker-Taylor. We then allow the distance distribution to change either according to a predetermined schedule or adaptively using the current permutation and the entire history. Matching upper and lower bounds show that both classes have optimal runtime $Θ(n(\log n)^2/\log\log n)$. Thus, scheduled adjustments of the distance distribution improve the optimal static worst-case runtime by a factor of $Θ(\log\log n)$, while full-information adaptation provides no further asymptotic improvement.

♻ ☆ Tight Bounds for $(1+ε)$-Approximation for Minimum Spanning Trees in Doubling Metrics SP
Jan Höckendorff, Felix Hommelsheim, Christian Sohler, Di Yue
The minimum spanning tree (MST) problem is one of the most basic optimization problems on metric spaces and graphs. We study the problem of computing a $(1+ε)$-approximation to the MST of an $n$-point metric space of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}$. In doubling metrics, previous deterministic algorithms incur a running time with dependence $ε^{-O(\mathrm{ddim})}$. We give a deterministic algorithm that computes a $(1+ε)$-approximate MST in time $$ O_{\mathrm{ddim}}\left(n\log n+ \min\left\{n^2,\frac{n}ε\log(1/ε)\right\}\right) $$ in the standard real RAM model with a unit-cost exact-distance oracle. For bounded doubling dimension, this improves the previous dependence on $ε$ to essentially linear in $ε^{-1}$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound of $$ Ω\!\left(n\log n+ \min\left\{n^2,\frac{n}ε\log(1/ε)\right\}\right) $$ on running time in the same model, already for metrics of doubling dimension at most seven, showing that our running time is essentially tight. For points in $\mathbb R^d$ with $d = O(1)$, exploiting Euclidean geometry allows us to further improve the dependence on $ε$. We obtain a $(1+ε)$-approximate MST in expected time $$ O_d\left( n \log n + \min\left\{n^2, \frac{n}{ε^{1 - β_d}} \log^{1-β_d}(1/ε) \right\} \right) $$ for some $β_d=Θ(1/d)$, improving the accuracy-dependent term $nε^{-2}\log^2(1/ε)$ of Arya and Mount [SODA'16].

♻ ☆ Improved Bounds for Directed SSSP in Sparse and Intermediate-Density Graphs
Valery, Grishin, Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy
We give a deterministic algorithm for exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) in directed graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and nonnegative real edge weights. When $m=O(n)$, it runs in $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4})$ time. For $m=Θ(n)$, this lowers the exponent of $\log\log n$ in the bound of Duan, Mao, Shu and Yin from $1/2$ to $1/4$. At intermediate densities, writing $d=m/n$, the same algorithm improves on the bound of Duan et al. when $d\geq 3$ and $d\log(2+d)=o(\log\log n)$. For example, when $m=Θ(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$, it runs in $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{5/8})$ time, lowering their exponent from $3/4$ to $5/8$.

♻ ☆ Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
Rick van der Heijden
This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.

♻ ☆ Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
Hendrik Molter
We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. We survey bounds that can be recovered from earlier work under FPT $\neq$ W[1] and prove seven lower bounds for graph problems and set systems under the same assumption. The new proofs encode clique choices in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of the encoding. This lets us turn a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem into a fixed-parameter algorithm for Clique or Multicolored Clique. In several cases, the new bound matches the function of the parameter in the historical exponent, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.
♻ ☆ Efficient Adaptive Data Analysis over Dense Data Distributions NeurIPS 2026
Joon Suk Huh
Modern data workflows are inherently adaptive, repeatedly querying the same dataset to refine and validate sequential decisions, but such adaptivity can lead to overfitting and invalid statistical inference. Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) mechanisms address this challenge; however, there is a fundamental tension between computational efficiency and sample complexity. For $T$ rounds of adaptive analysis, computationally efficient algorithms typically incur suboptimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ sample complexity, whereas for arbitrary distributions, algorithms with $O(\log T)$ sample complexity are computationally intractable under standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work, we shed light on this trade-off by identifying a natural class of data distributions under which both computational efficiency and logarithmic sample complexity in $T$ are achievable. We propose a computationally efficient ADA mechanism that attains $O(\log T)$ sample complexity, optimal in its dependence on $T$, when the data distribution is dense with respect to a known prior. This setting includes, in particular, feature-label data distributions arising in distribution-specific learning. As a consequence, our mechanism also yields a sample-efficient (i.e., $O(\log T)$ samples) statistical query oracle in the distribution-specific setting. Moreover, although our algorithm is not based on differential privacy, it satisfies a relaxed privacy notion known as Predicate Singling Out (PSO) security (Cohen and Nissim 2020) whenever the number of its possible update transcripts is polynomial in the sample size. Our results thus reveal an inherent connection between adaptive data analysis and privacy beyond differential privacy.
comment: 20 pages, NeurIPS 2026 Camera-ready, arXiv title corrected
♻ ☆ The Complexity of Computing Class Probabilities in BID Probabilistic Databases
Sotiris Kanellopoulos, Ioannis Koutras, Aris Pagourtzis
We study the problem of computing class probabilities in block-independent disjoint (BID) probabilistic databases. Given the probability with which each block in the database realizes each feasible tuple type, the goal is to compute the probability of a class of worlds specified by a given tuple multiplicity vector, thus grouping together worlds with the same bag (multiset) of realized tuple types. For this problem, we prove $\#\mathsf{P}$-hardness even for very restricted and structured inputs. On the other hand, we show that it admits an FPRAS, as well as $\mathsf{XP}$-time algorithms parameterized by the number of tuple types and the treewidth of an incidence graph modeling the connections between blocks and tuples. Finally, we show that augmenting the problem with certain compatibility constraints between block realizations renders it $\#\mathsf{XLP}$- and $\#\mathsf{XALP}$-hard parameterized by pathwidth and treewidth respectively, ruling out $\mathsf{FPT}$ algorithms under standard assumptions. We leave as an open question whether this also holds in the absence of compatibility constraints.
Graphics 5
☆ Where Does Personalization Reside in Photo Editing? Evidence from One Photographer's Lightroom History
Dongwu Qian
Personalized photo-editing systems must infer both a photographer's recurring preferences and the intent of a particular shoot, yet these signals are rarely evaluated separately. We study interpretable Lightroom adjustments in a longitudinal, private dataset of 3,193 edited photographs from 41 catalogs by one professional photographer, with holdouts formed at the batch level. We compare absolute and prior-relative targets, image-conditioned predictors, and estimators that receive a small set of edits from the target batch. Residual prediction improves validation error, but its advantage on held-out batches is small and not significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap (0.592 vs 0.582 EV exposure MAE). In a batch-shared protocol, closed-form shrinkage using 4, 8, or 16 same-batch anchors reaches 0.466, 0.457, or 0.453 EV with the best estimator at each k, compared with 0.586-0.592 EV for the prior-only baseline; the paired reductions are significant under a batch-clustered bootstrap. Learned anchor-conditioned heads do not improve on this closed-form estimator, and a negative-trained prior already yields a low cold-image false-edit rate, leaving little benefit for an additional gate. The recommended estimator is closed-form and auditable, and it requires only a handful of same-batch edits. A render-space check against 383 native Lightroom exports reproduces the ranking: at k=8, online EB lowers Delta E00 against the prior by 0.41 (p=0.042), and the photographer's true parameters lower it by 0.78 (p=0.034). An appendix extends the action space from six to thirteen global controls: a same-batch median look lowers rendered chroma toward the export, while a per-photograph residual head again fails to transfer. The study is limited to one photographer and does not claim that slider accuracy measures aesthetic preference.

☆ Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation via Topology-Aware Distillation and Progressive Kinematic Reasoning
Kanglei Zhou, Zikai Hao, Liyuan Wang, Xiaohui Liang
Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.

♻ ☆ SpA2V: Harnessing Spatial Auditory Cues for Audio-driven Spatially-aware Video Generation
Kien T. Pham, Yingqing He, Yazhou Xing, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen
Audio-driven video generation aims to synthesize realistic videos that align with input audio recordings, akin to the human ability to visualize scenes from auditory input. However, existing approaches predominantly focus on exploring semantic information, such as the classes of sounding sources present in the audio, limiting their ability to generate videos with accurate content and spatial composition. In contrast, we humans can not only naturally identify the semantic categories of sounding sources but also determine their deeply encoded spatial attributes, including locations and movement directions. This useful information can be elucidated by considering specific spatial indicators derived from the inherent physical properties of sound, such as loudness or frequency. As prior methods largely ignore this factor, we present SpA2V, the first framework explicitly exploits these spatial auditory cues from audios to generate videos with high semantic and spatial correspondence. SpA2V decomposes the generation process into two stages: 1) Audio-guided Video Planning: We meticulously adapt a state-of-the-art MLLM for a novel task of harnessing spatial and semantic cues from input audio to construct Video Scene Layouts (VSLs). This serves as an intermediate representation to bridge the gap between the audio and video modalities. 2) Layout-grounded Video Generation: We develop an efficient and effective approach to seamlessly integrate VSLs as conditional guidance into pre-trained diffusion models, enabling VSL-grounded video generation in a training-free manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpA2V excels in generating realistic videos with semantic and spatial alignment to the input audios.

♻ ☆ GraftRay: Physically Based Mesh Insertion into Gaussian Splatting Scenes via Path Tracing
Jinxin Ai, Matthias Nießner
We present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into 2D and 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) indoor scenes, accounting for lighting interactions between objects and their surroundings. We lift albedo, roughness, metallic and normals from diffusion-based 2D priors onto the Gaussians by back-projection, model windows and lamps as analytic area emitters, and recover their absolute radiance from ordinary LDR captures with a low-dimensional fit over unit-radiance bases. A path tracer over Gaussians and meshes then produces view-consistent shading, interreflections and soft shadows, which are composited onto the original reconstruction by differential rendering, preserving the untouched background. On synthetic, real and generated scenes, GraftRay outperforms recent insertion and inverse-rendering baselines in image fidelity and shadow accuracy at competitive cost, and users prefer its lighting and shadows over those of the baselines.

♻ ☆ IBPA: Real-time Free-form Manifold Mesh Reconstruction via Incremental Ball Pivoting with Integrated Hole Detection
Mauhing Yip, Mohit Singh, Kostas Alexis, Christian Schellewald, Annette Stahl
Both Remotely Operated underwater Vehicles (ROVs) and Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) are frequently deployed to acquire geometric bathymetric data. However, it is often discovered post-survey that the acquired data coverage is incomplete. Given the high operational cost associated with underwater deployments, it is essential to incrementally visualize surface coverage in real-time to support informed decision-making by both the operators of ROVs and the AUVs during data collection. In addition, traditional incremental surface reconstruction methods, such as Digital Terrain Models (DTMs), are inherently limited in expressiveness: they represent surfaces as height fields, allows only one elevation value per $(x, y)$ coordinate and thus cannot capture overhangs or vertical structures. To overcome these limitations, we adapt the original Ball Pivoting Algorithm (BPA) into an incremental, real-time, and free-form surface reconstruction method, referred to as Incremental BPA (IBPA). Our method incrementally constructs an orientable, manifold mesh from streaming point cloud data without imposing assumptions regarding point cloud overlap or spatial distribution. Furthermore, we introduce a hole detection mechanism that identifies and highlights incomplete mesh regions. Compared to existing approaches, our method supports more complex surface topologies without prior structural assumptions. The source code of our reference implementation is available: https://github.com/Mauhing/Incremental-BPA

♻ ☆ High-Throughput Private Information Retrieval with on-CPU Accelerators
Gyuyeong Kim
We present AltoPIR, the first PIR system that exploits the capability of emerging on-CPU matrix accelerators such as Intel AMX. Unlike existing solutions, AltoPIR achieves high-performance PIR through efficient batching without requiring discrete accelerators. However, the on-CPU accelerator has only a few small registers and shares its core with request handling. As a result, it runs far below its peak rate while its operands arrive from memory, and it remains idle while its core handles requests. To keep the accelerator busy, we design mechanisms that reduce both the memory traffic of a batch and the core cycles spent on each request. Our experimental results show that AltoPIR outperforms existing CPU-based solutions by up to 50.1x.

♻ ☆ TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect - KV Cache Management for AI Agents
Shashwat Jaiswal, Chloe Alverti, Mengmei Ye, Chen Wang, Hubertus Franke, Fan Lai, Tianyin Xu, Josep Torrellas
LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference. To address this problem, we present TripleKV, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory. Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45-76% to under 10%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7$\times$ lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.

☆ Multi-Order Passive Macromodeling from Layouts via Nested Port-Hamiltonian Learning
Benchao Zhu, Keren Zhu
Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).
☆ VEGA: A Scalable Software-Hardware Co-design for Genome Alignment using RVV Extension
Weihong Xu, Shijie Xu, Qunyou Liu, Giovanni Ansaloni, Cheng Zhuo, David Atienza
Dynamic programming (DP)-based genome sequence analysis is fundamental to computational genomics, but it remains computationally intensive as genomic data volumes continue to outpace Moore's Law. Existing hardware accelerators often sacrifice programmability and scalability across diverse alignment algorithms. In this work, we present VEGA, a scalable software-hardware co-design that accelerates genome alignment using RISC-V Vector extensions. VEGA introduces specialized vector instructions and three key innovations: a Forefront Stationary dataflow that minimizes off-chip memory access, intersequence parallelism that maximizes SIMD lane utilization, and custom ISA extensions that accelerate core alignment operations. Evaluations show that VEGA achieves up to 15.1x and 9.7x speedups for Edit Distance and Smith-Waterman algorithms over the Ara2-RVV vector baseline, sustaining 10.2x and 6.7x gains for 10kbp sequences. Post-synthesis results indicate only 1.0% area overhead compared to a standard RISC-V core, with performance-per-area efficiency rivaling specialized ASICs. VEGA thus achieves a balanced advancement in efficiency, programmability, and scalability for genome sequence alignment.
☆ QUISA: A Compact, Flexible and Unified Instruction-Set Coprocessor for QR-UOV Signature
Malik Imran, Ciara Rafferty, Ayesha Khalid, Maire O'Neill
QR-UOV is a Quotient Ring Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) multivariate quadratic (MQ) signature scheme that has progressed to round-3 of the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) additional signatures call by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Until now, for architectural efficiency and performance trade-offs, QR-UOV has been evaluated only on software platforms and has never been considered on hardware, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). To address this, we are the first to provide a complete QR-UOV hardware implementation through a flexible and unified QUISA coprocessor design, which supports instruction-driven execution for key generation, signing, and verification across all three NIST security levels (SL-I, SL-III, SL-V). The proposed architecture features extensive throughput optimizations by parallelizing key QR-UOV module operations, such as the pseudorandom byte generator, hashing, and rejection sampling. To minimize hardware resources, we propose a modular arithmetic unit with finite-field reduction based on the shift-add folding method. The design introduces a linear system solver for QUISA based on LU decomposition with partial pivoting and a sample solution module, operating over the prime field Fq (q = 127). We comprehensively evaluate QUISA on an Artix-7 FPGA at 80 MHz up to the post-place-and-route stage, utilizing 11,144 slices and 35,248 look-up tables. For higher SL-V security levels, it completes key generation, signing, and verification in 30.4M, 3.8M, and 2.8M clock cycles, respectively.

☆ When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
Feiyang Pan, Shenghe Zheng, Pengfei Xiao, Chunyan Yin, Guangbin Dou
Large language models (LLMs) can generate register-transfer-level (RTL) designs from natural-language specifications. To improve functional correctness, many RTL agents use simulation feedback to guide refinement. However, without a reference testbench, generating one for every initial implementation incurs inference cost even when the RTL is correct. We therefore introduce an adaptive harness that uses a specialized decision model to orchestrate testing, refinement, and candidate selection. It accepts high-scoring initial implementations and generates testbenches for the rest. When further search is needed, the initial score guides repair--regeneration allocation, while defect rankings and simulation feedback guide repair. For final selection, the harness prioritizes test-passing candidates and ranks them using decision-model scores. Across three benchmarks, the harness with DeepSeek improves mean Pass@1 by 5.4--7.1 percentage points over initial implementations and reduces aggregate estimated inference cost by 11.0--14.3% relative to a testbench-guided repair baseline with the same candidate cap.
☆ APUF-SNG: A Low-Cost Arbiter-PUF Stochastic Number Generator with Tunable Output Probability
Shelby Williams, Mehran Moghadam, M. Hassan Najafi, Sercan Aygun, Arman Roohi, Gourav Datta
Stochastic computing (SC) encodes numerical values as probabilistic bit-streams and enables arithmetic operations using simple logic gates, offering a promising paradigm for low- cost, fault-tolerant, and highly parallel computation. However, the accuracy and efficiency of SC systems depend on the quality of the stochastic number generator (SNG). Conventional SNGs rely on pseudo-random or quasi-random generators, whose deterministic nature introduces periodicity, correlation, and bias, limiting achievable accuracy and robustness. This paper proposes a low- cost arbiter physical unclonable function (APUF)-based SNG that operates in near-metastable delay conditions to generate true- random stochastic bit-streams with controllable output probabilities. By selecting input challenges that drive the path delay difference toward a target value, the resulting output probability is governed by intrinsic device noise, eliminating the need for conventional random-number generators and comparator-based SNGs. The proposed design inherits the low hardware overhead and statistical independence properties of the APUF structure. A probabilistic model and a challenge selection method are developed to characterize and control the stochastic behavior. An 8-stage APUF-SNG matches the 1% mean absolute error of state- of-the-art true-random SNGs at 1024-bit streams and occupies 116μm^2 in 45nm, 2.5x and 7x smaller than the TRNG-based and Sobol-based generator designs, respectively.
☆ Selective ROM Weight Storage for Responsive LLM Control on Edge Robots
Boxiang Song, Zhihong Chen, Xiaoyu Hao, Jinhong Huang, Chengkai Zhu, Jiaqi Yang, Hongyang Pan, Changhao Yan, Keren Zhu
Edge robots increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for complex tasks, demanding efficient inference alongside timely control. Limited memory capacity constrains model deployment, while repeated weight transfers during decoding compete with activations and KV cache for external bandwidth. Sequential generation of robot actions further delays decisions and periodic control on shared hardware. Experiments with Qwen3-8B achieve a peak decode speedup of 1.56$\times$ and reduce P99 task response time by a factor of approximately 227.27$\times$, while completing 100.00\% of the tested grasping and transport tasks.
☆ Reverse Seam-Carving: Structured Whitespace Preconditioning for Fixed-Die P&R
Andrew B. Kahng, Yiting Liu, Davit Markarian
At high placement utilization, limited whitespace increases cell displacement during legalization and clock tree synthesis (CTS), degrading routed wirelength. Existing P&R methodologies use uniform density targets or reactive whitespace redistribution, without optimizing whitespace structure before placement. We propose Reverse Seam-Carving (RSC), a pre-placement methodology that redistributes whitespace into core-spanning low-density seams between denser regions, while preserving die area and utilization. We further develop SeamGain, a semi-analytical model that selects the RSC configuration from a single reference run of the uniform flow; one SeamGain-selected run obtains 86% of the best-of-sweep wirelength reduction. In the OpenROAD flow with ASAP7, RSC achieves (maximum, average) post-route wirelength reductions of (27.6%, 15.4%).

♻ ☆ StreamingDPD: A 1.28-GSa/s Instantaneous-Power-Gated Depthwise TCN Accelerator for Real-Time 320-MHz Digital Predistortion
Yizhuo Wu, Xinling Wang, Chang Gao
State feedback between successive samples limits the streaming throughput of recurrent neural networks for digital predistortion (DPD). We present StreamingDPD, an accelerator that processes 320-MHz signals at 1.28 GSa/s. Its 207-parameter instantaneous-power-gated depthwise temporal convolutional network (IPG-DWTCN) uses $|x[n]|^2$ to gate feature channels and causal dilated depthwise convolutions to model power amplifier memory. The network maps to a spatially unrolled fixed-point pipeline with shift-based quadratic activations and layer-wise mixed precision, sustaining one complex sample per cycle per lane. Its algorithmic cost is 554 floating-point operations per complex sample, 30.1% fewer than the recurrent baseline with the best linearization performance. In RF playback measurements on three power amplifiers driven by 40- to 320-MHz Wi-Fi 6/7 and 5G NR waveforms, IPG-DWTCN achieves the lowest mean adjacent-channel power ratio (ACPR) and ranks first or ties for first in mean error vector magnitude (EVM) against five neural baselines of comparable size. Four-lane FPGA hardware-in-the-loop tests on a 320-MHz 4096-QAM Wi-Fi 7 waveform achieve -45.82 dBc ACPR and -42.94 dB EVM at 1.28 GSa/s. At the same sample rate, post-layout evaluation of a single-lane 12-nm FinFET ASIC yields a 0.10 mm$^2$ core, a 52-cycle (40.63 ns) latency, and an estimated typical-corner power of 142.21 mW (111.10 pJ/sample). Relative to the prior 22-nm recurrent DPD ASIC, the design provides 5.1 times the throughput at about one-seventh the energy per sample.

In all types of decoders, fully neural network-based high-level decoders offer decoding thresholds that surpass baseline decoder-Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM), and exhibit strong scalability, making them one of the ideal solutions for addressing surface code challenges. To address these challenges, we first propose a parallel fully feedforward neural network (FFNN) high-level surface code decoder, and comprehensively measure its decoding performance on a computing-in-memory (CIM) hardware simulation platform. With the currently available hardware specifications, our work achieves a decoding threshold of 14.22%, surpassing the MWPM baseline of 10.3%, and achieves high pseudo-thresholds of 10.4%, 11.3%, 12%, and 11.6% with decoding latencies of 197.03 ns, 234.87 ns, 243.73 ns, and 251.65 ns for distances of 3, 5, 7 and 9, respectively. The impact of hardware parameters and non-idealities on these results is discussed, and the hardware simulation results are extrapolated to a 4K quantum cryogenic environment.

Second, on 211 evaluable model--module entries in the deep subset, assertion sets flag buggy RTL with 0.87 recall, but 40\% of predicted-buggy outcomes are false positives on correct RTL, limiting precision to 0.60. Third, agentic mode improves S1-style provability and strength metrics, but gains plateau and oscillate. Codes and artifacts are available at \href{https://github.com/HierSVAAnon/HierSVACodeAndArtifacts}{https://github.com/HierSVAAnon/HierSVACodeAndArtifacts}. ♻ ☆ FoldSim: Scaling Cycle-Exact RTL Simulation with Hierarchical Folding and Static Scheduling
Chengxuan Wang, Nikhil Rout, Yang-gon Kim, Jacob Leigh, Yufan Du, Blaise Tine
RTL simulation is essential for hardware design and verification, yet its execution time grows rapidly with design scale and complexity. CPU- and GPU-based simulators exploit parallelism to accelerate RTL evaluation, but achieving high simulation throughput for large designs remains challenging. FPGA-based simulators offer higher throughput by mapping RTL computations directly onto hardware, but their scalability is constrained by FPGA resource capacity. We present FoldSim, an automated framework that enables cycle-exact simulation of large RTL designs on a single FPGA through hierarchical folding. FoldSim maps instances across the design hierarchy onto shared logic while maintaining their independent state. Given foldable module classes, its compiler constructs a static schedule that coordinates their execution, reducing dynamic synchronization overhead and making state accesses predictable. FoldSim backs state that exceeds on-chip capacity with external memory and brings it to the shared circuits as needed. A configurable DRAM model separates target-memory timing from host delays. The compiler explores replica allocations and state placement to balance resource savings against simulation time. On one AMD Alveo V80, FoldSim runs an 8-SM GPU and a 1,024-node Rocket datacenter with 4,096 processor cores. The unfolded implementations require approximately 16x and 200x as many LUTs as FoldSim's, respectively. The datacenter keeps about 1.9 GB of state in HBM, while a 4-SM GPU completes a 1024x1024 GEMM in 4.24 seconds, versus 26 hours in software RTL simulation.

☆ An End-to-End Theory for Compositional Symbolic Execution: From Expressive Specifications to SMT (Extended Version)
Shivanandan Tamil Kumaran, Andreas Lööw, Philippa Gardner
Compositional symbolic execution (CSE) is a powerful technique for program verification and bug-finding, yet existing formal theories of CSE do not sufficiently bridge the gap between idealised models and real-world tools. We present progress towards a foundational, realistic, end-to-end theory of CSE in the Rocq proof assistant. Our theory advances realism at both ends of the CSE pipeline: it supports an expressive frontend with algebraic data types, logical functions, and lemmas; it also provides a verified connection to SMT-LIB compliant SMT solvers. Our contributions include: (1) a CSE theory that captures practical verification patterns; (2) a standalone, reusable Rocq mechanisation of the SMT-LIB standard; (3) a proven-correct encoding from CSE backend queries to SMT-LIB queries that accounts for semantic discrepancies and optimises using type information; and (4) empirical evidence for the backend by extracting our verified SMT-LIB encoding and running it alongside the CSE tool Gillian's own encoding on a majority of its solver queries.
☆ Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
Leizhen Zhang, Sheng Chen
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

Parameter sensitivities of analog circuits enable the use of gradient-based design optimization methods and unlock a range of sensitivity analyses. Finite difference methods, which estimate gradients through simulation, require N + 1 to 2N simulations for each gradient depending on the method, which can become prohibitively expensive when many parameters are optimized. We use VAPY and Circulax to optimize three analog circuits implemented in the SkyWater SKY130 PDK, which is built on the BSIM4 device model. VAPY-generated model gradients closely match finite-difference gradients, achieving comparable design quality in over 40X fewer circuit solves and up to 40% lower loss than Bayesian optimization.

Gabriel Ebner
JIT compilers are among the most attacked components of modern software. They compile attacker-chosen programs, speculate on attacker-influenced type feedback, and run the result at full native privilege. A single wrongly eliminated guard or a missing deoptimization becomes memory corruption. We present SafeJIT, a small JavaScript engine with a speculating baseline JIT, together with a machine-checked proof in Lean 4 that its statically linked RISC-V and x86-64 executables never crash, on any input, in a model of a Linux user process. The theorem is about the shipped binaries, executed instruction by instruction on Sail ISA models (for RISC-V, the official one), and it covers everything in them: the parser and bytecode compiler, the interpreter and its type-feedback recording, the JIT compiler, all machine code the JIT can generate for any program and any feedback (type guards, guard elimination, loop type facts, register allocation with deoptimization metadata, inline caches, deoptimization and on-stack replacement), a mark-sweep garbage collector, the runtime, and a freestanding libc. The C compiler, assembler and linker are not trusted, and neither is floating-point arithmetic. The proof uses separation logic (iris-lean) over a model of a Linux user process whose stuck states are exactly the ways a process can crash, including fetching code that has not been made executable or whose instruction cache has not been flushed.
♻ ☆ VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
Manish Acharya, Zhenyu Liao, Yueke Zhang, Kevin Leach, Yu Huang, Yifan Zhang
LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.
♻ ☆ When the Next Step Is Not One Step: Distribution-Aware Execution Modeling for Concurrent Go Programs
Kaviru Hapuarachchi
Predicting the next scheduler event of a concurrent program is ill-posed as single-label classification: repeated runs from the same trace prefix produce different, equally valid next events. We formulate next-event prediction for concurrent Go programs as estimating an empirical next-event distribution obtained from repeated executions, and release a benchmark with 945 training examples from hand-written and generated programs and 798 held-out predictions on 54 real-world GoKer bug kernels from systems such as CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC and etcd. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with low-rank adapters under a cross-entropy objective and a KL-to-empirical-distribution objective and compare them with zero-shot models and trivial baselines. The outcome is a neutral-to-negative result. The fine-tuned adapters (re-evaluated: 36.3% cross-entropy, 33.6% KL; originally reported 36.2% and 35.8%) are statistically indistinguishable from always predicting the majority event (35.5%), and an event n-gram model reaches 33-34%. Because each held-out prompt carries labels from about five runs, no deterministic predictor can exceed 58.9% top-1 accuracy, so we report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, program-clustered confidence intervals and binned calibration measured directly on both adapters. A sensitivity study with 100 runs per program shows that five-run targets are noisy (mean total-variation distance 0.24 from a 100-run reference), which plausibly limits what the KL objective can learn. Rare event types are essentially never predicted. A select-block goroutine-leak signature follows from scheduler semantics rather than learning. We release the data, adapters and tooling.

♻ ☆ Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
Yusen Su, Jorge A. Navas, Arie Gurfinkel
Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis. To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.

☆ Algorithms for Collaborative Truck-Multi-Drone Delivery in the En-Route Model
Jerry Mathew Oommen, Kelin Luo
We study collaborative truck--multi-drone delivery in the en-route model, in which a truck moves continuously along a fixed straight-line path while drones serve $n$ off-route deliveries. For maximum coverage with $k$ drones, we prove that Sequential Greedy achieves an approximation guarantee of $1-(k/(k+1))^k$, which approaches $1-e^{-1}$. For $k=2$, our analysis is tight, with a matching $5/9$ instance. We refute the claimed exchange property for proper instances. For a new class of swap-monotone instances with distinct $x$-coordinates, we give an exact $O(n^2)$-time dynamic program for single-drone maximum coverage. For minimum fleet size, we prove NP-hardness and give an $O(1+\log(n/k^\ast))$-approximation using an integer residual bound, where $k^\ast$ is the optimum fleet size.

☆ A Simple Optimal Algorithm for Directed Multi-Failure Replacement Paths
Kaito Harada, Tatsuya Terao
Given a graph $G = (V, E)$ and two vertices $s, t \in V$, the $f$-fault replacement paths ($f$-FRP) problem asks to compute, for every set $F$ of at most $f$ edges, the distance from $s$ to $t$ in $G \setminus F$. In this paper, we present a $3$-FRP algorithm in deterministic $O(n^3 \log n)$ time for directed weighted graphs. We also present a deterministic $O(n^4)$ time algorithm for $4$-FRP in directed weighted graphs, which implies a deterministic $O(n^f)$ time algorithm for $f$-FRP for every $f \ge 4$. Since the output size of $f$-FRP can be $Θ(n^f)$, our algorithms are optimal for every $f \ge 4$ and nearly optimal for $f = 3$. Our algorithms also extend to the single-source and all-pairs settings with $f-1$ and $f-2$ failures, respectively, with the same time complexity as $f$-FRP. Moreover, our algorithms are remarkably simple.

☆ Exact edge cover by strict and non-strict temporal walks
Duc Thien Quach, Manh Cuong Tran
Exact edge cover asks whether the edges of a temporal graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges can be partitioned into time-respecting walks with a prescribed number of walks starting at each vertex and, in the fixed-end variant, ending at each vertex. For non-strict walks, we prove that the problem is polynomially solvable by a new approach based on M-convexity, which also closes a gap in the proof sketch of an earlier static reduction. An orientation of the edges is realizable by walks exactly when walk counters stay non-negative and every snapshot component contains a walk, and only components with all degrees and counters even can violate the latter condition. Once a dead state is removed, the states of each such component form an M-convex set. This yields an augmenting path algorithm that returns walks or an infeasibility certificate, using at most $m/2$ augmentations and $O(n+nm^2)$ arithmetic operations with path-reversing re-orientation. The implementation was validated on small instances. For strict walks, we prove that the problem is NP-complete, already with six time labels for prescribed ends and two for free ends.
☆ Towards a faster parameterized algorithm for Chordal Vertex Deletion

The \textsc{Chordal Vertex Deletion} (\chvd{}) problem asks whether an input graph $G$ can be made chordal by removing at most $k$ vertices. When $k$ is taken as parameter, this problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable \cite{M10,CM16}. However, it is still open whether \chvd{} admits a single-exponential FPT algorithm, i.e. an algorithm with running time $O(α^k |V(G)|^c)$ for some constant $α$ independent of $k$. Towards this goal, we describe an FPT algorithm for the compression version of \chvd{} with the following specification. Given an instance $I = (G,k,X)$ of the disjoint \chvd{} compression problem such that $|X| = k+1$, $G - X$ is chordal and its longest chordless path has length $L$, we solve $I$ in time $O((L+1)^{3k} k^2 |V(G)|^4)$.

☆ String Indexing for Maximal Gap-Bounded Occurrence Clusters
Waseem Akram, Takuya Mieno
Repeated occurrences of a pattern can form groups that reveal where repetition is concentrated in a text. We study how to find such groups efficiently when both the pattern $P$ and the distance threshold $G$ between occurrences are specified as query parameters. A maximal $G$-cluster of $P$ is a maximal block of at least two occurrences of $P$ whose consecutive starting positions differ by at most $G$. In this paper, we present indexes for reporting all cluster intervals and counting the clusters. For a text of length $n$ and a pattern of length $m$, we propose an $O(n\log n)$-space index that reports all maximal cluster intervals in $O(m+\log\log n+\mathit{output})$ time, where $\mathit{output}$ is the number of reported intervals, and that counts the clusters in $O(m+\log\log n)$ time. Restricting occurrences to those fully contained in a query substring preserves the reporting time using $O(n\log^2 n)$ space. Our indexes combine suffix-tree decompositions with geometric reporting queries on consecutive gaps.

☆ Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
Moïse Blanchard, Ezra Edelman, Surbhi Goel, Shyam Narayanan, Jialin Yu
We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

☆ A $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-Approximation for Weighted 3-Set Packing
Changjun Wang, Daorong Yu, Wei Yu
We give a deterministic $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted $3$-set packing, for every fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$, improving on the 1.6908-approximation reported by Tong and Xu (2026). The algorithm has two phases. It first performs bounded local search using a rounded $12/7$-power potential. It then combines compatible exchanges that insert at most three sets and increase the original weight. The analysis relates the gap left by the first phase to the gain available to the second phase. We prove a structural inequality that bounds the weight of a comparison packing by $3/2$ times the current weight plus one sixth of a sum of small-exchange gains. Each gain accounts for all sets that the exchange must delete. A greedy rule recovers enough of these gains to obtain the approximation guarantee. We derive the structural bound from local optimality by analyzing finite computation trees and averaging the error caused by their limited depth. The running time is $n^{4^{O(1/\varepsilon)}}\operatorname{poly}(L)$, where $n$ is the number of input sets and $L$ is the input encoding length. The same guarantee holds for maximum-weight independent set in induced $K_{1,4}$-free graphs.
♻ ☆ LLM Query Scheduling with Prefix Reuse and Latency Constraints NeurIPS 2025
Gregory Dexter, Shao Tang, Ata Fatahi Baarzi, Qingquan Song, Tejas Dharamsi, Aman Gupta
The efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) in online settings requires optimizing inference performance under stringent latency constraints, particularly the time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). This paper focuses on the query scheduling problem for LLM inference with prefix reuse, a technique that leverages shared prefixes across queries to reduce computational overhead. Our work reveals previously unknown limitations of the existing first-come-first-serve (FCFS) and longest-prefix-match (LPM) scheduling strategies with respect to satisfying latency constraints. We present a formal theoretical framework for LLM query scheduling under RadixAttention, a prefix reuse mechanism that stores and reuses intermediate representations in a radix tree structure. Our analysis establishes the NP-hardness of the scheduling problem with prefix reuse under TTFT constraints and proposes a novel scheduling algorithm, $k$-LPM, which generalizes existing methods by balancing prefix reuse and fairness in query processing. Theoretical guarantees demonstrate that $k$-LPM achieves improved TTFT performance under realistic traffic patterns captured by a data generative model. Empirical evaluations in a realistic serving setting validates our findings, showing significant reductions in P99 TTFT compared to baseline methods.

♻ ☆ Learn to Vaccinate: Combining Structure Learning and Effective Vaccination for Epidemic and Outbreak Control
Sepehr Elahi, Paula Mürmann, Patrick Thiran
The Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model is a widely used model for the spread of information and infectious diseases, particularly non-immunizing ones, on a graph. Given a highly contagious disease, a natural question is how to best vaccinate individuals to minimize the disease's extinction time. While previous works showed that the problem of optimal vaccination is closely linked to the NP-hard Spectral Radius Minimization (SRM) problem, they assumed that the graph is known, which is often not the case in practice. In this work, we consider the problem of minimizing the extinction time of an outbreak modeled by an SIS model where the graph on which the disease spreads is unknown and only the infection states of the vertices are observed. To this end, we split the problem into two: learning the graph and determining effective vaccination strategies. We propose a novel inclusion-exclusion-based learning algorithm and, unlike previous approaches, establish its sample complexity for graph recovery. We then detail an optimal SRM algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the number of vertices for bounded treewidth and a fixed vaccination budget. This is complemented by an efficient and effective polynomial-time greedy heuristic for any graph. Finally, we present experiments on synthetic and real-world data that numerically validate our learning and vaccination algorithms.

♻ ☆ Learning-Augmented Online Minimization with Dual Predictions
Christian Coester, Alexa Tudose, Alexander Turoczy
We present learning-augmented algorithms for two general classes of online minimization problems: metrical task systems and laminar set cover. Both algorithms achieve improved theoretical guarantees using machine-learned predictions of an optimal solution to the dual linear program. Unlike optimal primal solutions, which can change drastically under tiny instance perturbations, these dual solutions are much more stable, which ensures the existence of good (and learnable) predictions for families of similar instances. While previous work has used dual predictions in offline settings and for online maximization problems, our algorithms are, to the best of our knowledge, the first demonstration that such dual predictions can be effective for online minimization. Our theoretical results are complemented by experiments on the $k$-server problem and the parking permit problem.
♻ ☆ Closed Repeats
Dmitry Kosolobov
Much research in stringology focuses on structures that can, in a way, ``grasp'' repeats (substrings that occur multiple times) as, for example, the so-called runs, a.k.a. maximal repetitions, compactly describe all tandem repeats. In this paper we introduce closed repeats: given a string $s$, its non-empty substring $s[i\,..\,j]$ is a right (left) closed repeat if its closest occurrence $s[i'\,..\,j']$ with $i' > i$ cannot be ``extended'' to the right (respectively, left) matching $s[j{+}1] = s[j'{+}1]$ (respectively, $s[i{-}1] = s[i'{-}1]$); the repeat is closed if it is both left and right closed. We note that the closed repeats correspond to the maximal closed substrings recently proposed by Badkobeh, De Luca, Fici, and Puglisi and they include all runs as a special case. We prove that the number of right/left closed repeats is $O(n \log n)$, where $n$ is the length of $s$, and we show that this bound is tight. The (right/left) closed repeats can be computed in the optimal time $O(n\log n)$; as we prove, the time cannot be lower than $Ω(n\logσ)$ over a general size-$σ$ alphabet even if there are only $O(n)$ closed repeats. As an application, we describe data structures using the closed repeats for substring queries: finding the period of the substring provided it is ``periodic'', finding the longest repeat in the substring, computing the rightmost LZ77 parsing of the substring.

♻ ☆ Four Ways to Stream: Exponential Separations from Random Order and Quantum Memory
Nadezhda Voronova
A streaming algorithm can keep classical or quantum memory, and its input arrives in adversarial or random order. Each resource alone is known to beat the basic model exponentially, but it was not known whether random order can help a quantum algorithm. We compare the four models by exponential space separations: every pair is separated on some problem and tied on another, and the two models with one resource each beat each other on different problems, one direction for random inputs, by concurrent work of Bouland, Ding, and Jain. The new phenomenon is that quantum memory and random order together can be exponentially stronger than each alone. We show this on a streaming version of Hidden Matching in which the bits of $x\in\{0,1\}^N$ arrive many times and $m\le\sqrt{N}$ matching requests must be answered on arrival. In random order a quantum algorithm uses $O(\log N\log m)$ space, while classical algorithms need $Ω(\sqrt{N})$, and quantum algorithms need $Ω(m)$ when all data comes before the requests. Two properties explain this. Consumability: answering a request destroys the quantum state. Replenishment: the state can be rebuilt from bits that keep arriving, which random order supplies and a data-first order does not. We prove that one quantum message answering $m$ Hidden Matching requests needs $Ω(m)$ qubits, a conjecture of Gilboa, Jain, and McClean, for $m\le N^{1/2-δ}$. The rest comes from Noisy Gap Cycle, a problem of Assadi and Sundaresan: tell whether a graph is a union of cycles of length $k$ or $2k$. With long cycles it needs linear space in all four models: we extend their random-order lower bound to quantum algorithms and obtain the first quantum random-order lower bounds for natural graph problems. With short cycles, $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ classical bits suffice in random order, but adversarial order requires polynomial quantum space.

☆ Learning How a Body Moves: Few-Shot Body Inference for Visual World Models of Animated Characters
Amarnath R
Two visually identical animated characters can respond differently to the same action command because their body dynamics differ. For example, a stiff blob and its bouncy twin reach different heights when both receive the jump command. Given only the first frame and the action command, a visual world model has no information to distinguish these twins, because their initial appearances are identical. We therefore propose an in-context world model that encodes clips of a character's other actions into a body representation, using a contrastive loss to separate look-alike characters. We introduce ToonTwins, a benchmark of 144 2D cartoon characters that run, jump, fall, turn and crouch. Its characters form look-alike groups of four that differ only in their dynamics profile, and we also evaluate the model on 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D. Even with a body code from these clips, the latent pixel world model we tested recovered at most 25 percent of the twins' jump height difference. On new shapes, our model identified the correct twin in 85.9 percent of cases, compared with 76.7 percent for a transformer baseline that reads the same clips without a body summary, and in a controlled ablation the contrastive loss gave more than half of this gain. On the animated animals, it reduced the mean path prediction error by 8.5 percent against a model without body information.

Boyi Zhu, Youcheng Cai, Dong Wang
Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

Video world models enable interactive exploration of dynamic environments, yet struggle to respect prior observations over long horizons and across viewpoints. We present WorldCrafter, a video world model that learns a camera-queryable implicit 3D-aware memory for this purpose. The key insight is to let the requested viewpoint shape how multi-view evidence is compressed into the video generator's limited token budget. Trained jointly with the video generator, a memory encoder and pose-conditioned readout module integrate historical observations into a fixed set of target view-specific tokens before denoising, without explicit depth-based correspondences. By combining this memory with recent temporal context and few-step distillation, WorldCrafter enables streaming scene exploration from a single input image or text prompt. Experiments across static and dynamic scenes show substantial gains in long-horizon consistency and camera-control accuracy while preserving visual quality during minute-scale exploration.

☆ A code-level survey of CPU scheduling mechanisms in open-source embedded hypervisors
Lisa Mignerey, Anthony Ferrari, Damien Sauveron, Karim Tamine
Virtualization is increasingly used in embedded systems to consolidate mixed-criticality applications onto a single platform, relying on the hypervisor's CPU scheduler to share physical CPU (pCPU) time among virtual CPUs (vCPUs). This paper surveys ten CPU scheduling algorithms implemented in four open-source hypervisors for resource-constrained systems (Bao, Xen, ACRN, and Xvisor): static partitioning, ARINC653, Credit, Credit2, RTDS, Priority-based, BVT, IORR, PRR, and PRM. Analyzed at the source-code level without runtime measurements, each algorithm is characterized by its decision rule, parameters, selection criterion, triggers, and admission control. They are evaluated against nine criteria (temporal isolation, real-time guarantees, I/O responsiveness, resource utilization, fairness, mixed-criticality support, efficiency/scalability, configurability, and multicore support) and illustrated on a common single-pCPU workload. Source-code inspection reveals key deviations from documented designs: ACRN's default BVT scheduler lacks the warp mechanism, its priority-based scheduler exposes only two priority levels, and apart from ARINC653's static frame check, only Xen's development-branch RTDS performs utilization-based admission control. Furthermore, no policy natively supports criticality attributes or mode changes, requiring integrators to encode criticality via partitions, budgets, caps, or priorities. Finally, a qualitative matrix and a decision tree guide system integrators.
☆ Bring Cloud-Native Networking to FreeBSD Jails: Porting Calico from Linux
Soma Sakaguchi, Shintaro Suzuki, Yuki Nakata, Katsuya Matsubara
While Linux containers benefit from a rich ecosystem of Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins such as Calico and Cilium, FreeBSD Jails lacked native, standardized solutions for advanced networking. As a result, users have relied on manual, error-prone configurations, limiting scalability and integration with modern orchestration platforms. This paper introduces porting Calico, a widely adopted CNI plugin, to the FreeBSD operating system. Our approach replaced Linux-specific components with FreeBSD-native equivalents: iptables with ipfw, netlink sockets with routing sockets, and Linux network namespaces with FreeBSD's vnet. This work aims to bridge the gap between Linux and BSD container networking. By providing scalable, policy-driven capabilities that are compatible with existing Linux-centric infrastructure, FreeBSD can participate more fully in the broader container networking ecosystem.

☆ Self-Hosted WebAssembly Runtime for Runtime-Neutral Checkpoint/Restore in Edge-Cloud Continuum
Yuki Nakata, Katsuya Matsubara
Checkpoint/restore (C/R) in the Edge-Cloud Continuum, where edge servers and cloud servers are integrated to combine their respective computational characteristics, enables application live migration for load balancing and service continuity that adapts to user mobility. WebAssembly (Wasm) provides architecture neutrality, allowing bytecode execution across diverse platforms. Furthermore, by leveraging runtime implementations specialized for particular environments and performance optimizations such as JIT and AOT, Wasm bytecode can be executed efficiently by using the runtime best suited to each environment. However, the diversity of runtimes and performance optimizations results in heterogeneous representations of application execution states, making it difficult to apply C/R across multiple runtimes. To address this heterogeneity, we propose a C/R method that employs a self-hosted Wasm runtime compiled into Wasm itself. By checkpointing and restoring application execution states within the self-hosted Wasm runtime, the representation of execution states can be unified. In addition, to mitigate the overhead of duplicated runtime executions, we also investigate optimization techniques for Wasm runtimes designed to be self-hosted. Our evaluation results demonstrate that C/R with a self-hosted Wasm runtime can eliminate runtime differences and enable efficient live migration with a minimal execution state.

☆ Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

☆ FOREST: Coordinating Tree-based HBF, RRAM, and HBM for Efficient Speculative LLM Inference
Hao Ding, Zheng Shi, Dongxue Zhao, Huiying Bian, Meng Li, Xu Zheng, Kun Wang, Nanjian Wu, Jie Chen, Yimao Cai
Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by combining lightweight drafting with parallel target-model verification. However, its stages impose distinct resource demands: target verification requires high-throughput access to large weight sets, sequential drafting executes a compact model under tight latency constraints, and long-context attention processes growing key-value (KV) caches. Evaluated across six SD configurations spanning 32B-405B target models, FOREST achieves up to 5.5x end-to-end speedup, 11.46x higher decode throughput, and 16.5x higher decode energy efficiency over NVIDIA A800 GPU-based SD baselines. ☆ Acceleration of Sparse and Irregular Workloads through Energy-Efficient Stream Extensions

The slowdown of Moore's law and Dennard scaling has motivated computer architects to uphold performance scaling through architectural specialization. So far, most efforts have focused on highly regular workloads, which exhibit good data locality, ample reuse, and a data-independent execution flow. As this specialization hits diminishing returns, attention shifts towards sparse and irregular workloads, which are essential to applications like sparse neural networks, multiphysics simulations, and graph analytics. However, they lack the convenient properties of highly regular compute that modern architectures are optimized for, resulting in very low (<10%) functional unit utilization on traditional CPUs and GPUs. The most promising approaches to their general hardware acceleration leverage memory streams, which decouple data movement from execution. In this thesis, we explore energy-efficient hardware stream extensions that significantly accelerate sparse and irregular workloads in general-purpose systems without specializing to specific application domains or compromising on regular-workload performance. We design a flexible, core-coupled stream extension supporting affine and indirect streams as well as intersection and union of sparse tensors. We integrate it into an energy-efficient RISC-V compute cluster, achieving significant performance and energy efficiency benefits on general sparse linear algebra, and further use it to accelerate stencil computations, spiking neural network inference, and model-predictive control. We evaluate it at scale in a 432-core 2.5D RISC-V system fabricated in 12nm FinFET, achieving leading compute utilization and energy efficiency on sparse and irregular workloads while remaining competitive on regular workloads. Finally, we extend chip-level interconnects with end-to-end irregular streams, improving performance, energy efficiency, and bus utilization.

We evaluate SWAPPER at both component and application levels: at the component level, it reduces the mean absolute error by up to 50%, and at the application level it achieves up to 90% error reduction for AxBench suite and 66.7% top-1 improvement on a Vision Transformer.

Recently, the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT of OpenAI and Anthropic refuted ETH itself. Our main result transfers running times from 3-SAT to Cluster Editing. If 3-SAT on formulas with $m$ clauses can be decided in time $T(m)$, then there is an algorithm that, given a graph with $n$ vertices and integers $k$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le k^{1/3}$, decides Cluster Editing in time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot T(2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$. Combined with the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT, this proves Cao and Chen's conjecture, as it solves Cluster Editing in time $2^{O(k\cdot(\log\log\log k)^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log k})}\cdot n^{O(1)}=2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$. The key ingredient is a sparsification theorem for Cluster Editing, the counterpart of the Sparsification Lemma for satisfiability: In time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$, it reduces a given instance to $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}$ weighted instances with $O(rk)$ vertices and degree $O(r)$, each of which is equivalent to a 3-SAT formula with $2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k$ clauses. Conversely, by a known reduction with linear blow-up, every saving in the exponent for Cluster Editing is, up to constant factors, a saving for 3-SAT.
